abstract: |
  Video game research often treats games as a monolithic category, and single-game or single-platform studies leave open whether findings generalise across the medium. In this Registered Report, we used digital trace data from the Open Play dataset to test whether (H1) total playtime is meaningfully associated with mental wellbeing and (H2) this association differs by game genre. The data comprise 226,000 hours of playtime across 4,152 games from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam for 1,608 UK and US adults, linked to genre metadata and 6,293 biweekly wellbeing assessments (SWEMWBS). Judged against a preregistered threshold for practical significance, neither within-person fluctuations nor habitual differences in total playtime were meaningfully linked to wellbeing. The preregistered joint test found within-person differences between genres under our multi-genre attribution but not under the preregistered single-genre attribution, and no between-person differences. Under an exploratory hierarchical model, the estimated spread of the within-person genre effects implied that fewer than one of the 14 genres was expected to lie more than 0.06 points per hour from the average genre effect, and a multi-membership model estimated the spread less precisely. An exploratory daily-timescale analysis gave the same picture for total playtime and the hierarchical model's genre spread. Genre differences appear to be the wrong place to look for gaming's wellbeing effects, as genre labels are too coarse a proxy for the psychological experiences that plausibly drive them. We therefore regard finer-grained characterisations of play as the more promising avenue for further study.

# Introduction

Identifying how different types of games and gameplay affect wellbeing is vital in light of the contrast between popular sentiment, which treats video games as a harm to those who play them in the latest of a long line of technology panics [@orbenSisypheanCycleTechnology2020], and empirical evidence that playtime in general is not a meaningful predictor of wellbeing, using data from both specific games [@larrieuHowGamingMotives2023] and platforms [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. A common objection to these null findings is that the effect of play must depend on which games people play. Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain why aggregate playtime is poorly predictive of wellbeing, including displacement of beneficial activities, satisfaction or frustration of basic psychological needs, and selection effects whereby individuals with lower wellbeing play more [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. Displacement aside, these mechanisms operate at the level of game features or player experience rather than at the level of total time spent; playtime might be, at best, a moderator [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. In causal terms, playing is a compound exposure that comes in many versions, so an average association across all of them answers an ambiguous question [@magnusson2024harmful].

Given the vast heterogeneity between games, our understanding of the psychological processes and outcomes of digital play has been limited by video game effects research's widespread use of either undifferentiated self-report data, or digital trace data focusing on a single game or a handful of games [@bruhlmannMotivationalProfilingLeague2020; @JohannesEtAl2021video; @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022; @larrieuHowGamingMotives2023; @vuorreAffectiveUpliftVideo2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. While understandable given the limited resources and lack of objective data available to independent researchers, this narrow scope has left the field guessing whether identified relationships are unique to the studied titles or whether they apply universally across games. One step forward is therefore to capture comprehensive play behaviour data across the varied games and gaming platforms users regularly engage in, and to differentiate games using structured taxonomies. The most widespread system for classifying games is game genres, albeit not without some controversy [@clarkeWhyVideoGame2017; @vargas-iglesiasMakingSenseGenre2020; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024].

## Game Genres and Wellbeing

Consistent null findings for the effects of playtime on wellbeing have generated calls for the unpacking of raw decontextualised playtime into more informative measures that consider games' varied characteristics and affordances [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024]. Game genres offer a structured way to differentiate between video games and their corresponding play experiences [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. Genre differences in player behaviour, cognition, and gaming disorder symptoms are often proposed [@andreRelationshipGameGenre2024; @dobrowolskiCognitiveEnhancementVideo2015; @raithMassivelyMultiplayerOnline2021; @hazelExploringPossibleMental2022]: for example, action games have been linked to increased visual attention [@palausNeuralBasisVideo2017], cognitive and attentional control [@angueraVideoGameTraining2013; @bavelierEnhancingAttentionalControl2019], and working memory [@blackerEffectsActionVideo2014]. Massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs), first-person shooters, real-time strategy games (RTS), and Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games have been associated with higher gaming disorder symptoms [@elliottContributionGameGenre2012; @naInfluenceGameGenre2017; @kingMaladaptivePlayergameRelationships2019; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021]. Player experience also differs by genre: MOBA players report less immersion and autonomy and more frustration than players of single-player genres [@johnsonAllThatBase2015a], and role-playing games are the genre players most often perceive as beneficial [@hazelExploringPossibleMental2022]. Randomised controlled trials with casual games and exergames induced positive moods and reduced stress [@huangImpactPlayingExergames2017; @russonielloEffectivenessCasualVideo2009]. These findings suggest that the effects of video games are not uniform and that genre differences exist in both gaming behaviour and its impact on wellbeing. This evidence is, however, between-person: the observational studies compare people who favour different genres, and the trials assign people to one genre for a short period, so to our knowledge no study has asked whether a person's wellbeing rises and falls with their own genre playtime over time.

With more than 10,000 new games released each year [@notisYoureRightThere2021], an accessible classification system is essential for studying and comparing video games at scale. Genres, while defined by convention and neither exclusive nor exhaustive as labels [@clarkeWhyVideoGame2017; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @vargas-iglesiasMakingSenseGenre2020], remain the most pragmatic means of categorising video games. Psychologists have differentiated games based on genre for decades [@griffithsAreComputerGames1993; @wolf6GenreVideo2002], but must negotiate challenges in definition, overlaps between genres, and the continuous evolution of genres as new games are released. The overlaps are not a marginal problem: in metadata databases such as IGDB, most of the games people play carry more than one genre label (see Methods), which complicates any analysis that files each game under a single genre. Genre labels conflate distinct facets of games, such as gameplay style, purpose, and mood [@leeFacetAnalysisVideo2014], and factor-analytic decompositions of crowd-sourced game tags produce genre structures that diverge from conventional labels [@liFactororientedUnderstandingVideo2020]. Even the cognitive literature that produced the best-known genre-specific claims now treats genre labels as a weak proxy for the mechanics that matter, because games increasingly blend mechanics across genres, as popular titles such as *Skyrim* do [@bavelierEnhancingAttentionalControl2019]. Genres are therefore best treated not as definitive taxonomical statements but as crude yet practical tools for organising a growing and diversifying library.

There is a lack of consistent standardisation of game genres, leading to inconsistent classification of video game genres across psychological research [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024 counted 46 distinct taxonomies across the 96 articles they examined; only 50 articles (52%) drew on an existing or combined source for their classification, and 18 (19%) did not specify how their categories were constructed at all. Genre classifications are typically self-reported by participants or assigned by authors, and the same games are habitually classified into different genres across studies. This subjectivity undermines the validity of existing self-report or researcher-ascribed genre taxonomies for the meaningful comparison of results across studies.

Structured, crowd-sourced metadata repositories such as SteamDB, The Games Database, and the Internet Games Database (IGDB) offer a more reliable alternative, involving both game developers and large player samples in collaboratively maintaining genre labels [@liPreliminaryNetworkAnalysis2020; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @leeEmpiricalEvaluationMetadata2015]. Within the constraints of genre as a means of categorising games, metadata repositories best accommodate the fluidity of genres over time [@cohenHistoryGenre1986] and enable comparative research at scale.

## The Present Study

In line with prior evidence [@larrieuHowGamingMotives2023; @ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025], our first hypothesis predicts the absence of a meaningful relationship between playtime and wellbeing, now with digital trace data across several platforms and thousands of games:

**H1.** Total cross-platform playtime is not meaningfully associated with fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (**H1a**, "within-person") or with average wellbeing over the full study period (**H1b**, "between-person").

In practical terms, with H1a we ask whether a participant's wellbeing in a given two-week wave deviates from their own average when their playtime in that wave does, and with H1b whether participants who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than those who play less. Fluctuations in H1 therefore refer to deviations from a person's own average rather than to changes between consecutive waves. What counts as a meaningful association is fixed in advance by the smallest effect size of interest defined in the Methods.

Second, following previous literature [@andreRelationshipGameGenre2024; @dobrowolskiCognitiveEnhancementVideo2015; @raithMassivelyMultiplayerOnline2021; @hazelExploringPossibleMental2022; @elliottContributionGameGenre2012; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021], we predict that genres vary in their relation to wellbeing, with some potentially positive and others potentially negative, varying in strength. Put more formally:

**H2.** Genres differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (**H2a**, "within-person") and to average wellbeing over the full study period (**H2b**, "between-person").

With H2a we ask: when a participant plays more than their own average this wave, does it matter what genres that extra playtime is in? With H2b we ask the between-person complement: among people who play more overall, does it matter whether that habitual extra playtime is concentrated in, for example, RPGs versus Shooters versus other genres? By examining heterogeneity across genres [@vuorreCommunicatingCausalEffect2024], we thus test with H2 whether it is justified to generalise video game effects across genres, the generalisability that single-title studies sometimes assume [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022].

Beyond the preregistered hypotheses, we report one exploratory extension that was not preregistered. The biweekly window comprises potentially many individual play sessions and a single retrospective wellbeing judgement, so the preregistered tests leave open whether associations operate on shorter timescales. As such, we re-examine both hypotheses at the daily level.

```{r}
    mutate(date = as.Date(day_local))
)

platform_ranges <- map_dfr(names(telemetry_files), function(p) {
  tibble(
    platform = p,
    min_date = min(telemetry_files[[p]]$date, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_date = max(telemetry_files[[p]]$date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}) |>
  mutate(range_text = glue("{format(min_date, '%b %Y')} to {format(max_date, '%b %Y')}"))

telemetry_range_sentence <- platform_ranges |>
  mutate(platform_range = glue("{platform} ({range_text})")) |>
  pull(platform_range) |>
  paste(collapse = ", ")

# Intake window of the study proper, taken over qualified intakes (Nick
# Ballou, v4.1 review: recruitment closed 9 June 2025). Release v1.2.1 also
# held 2,324 ineligible post-closing intake rows (Jun 2025 to Jan 2026), none
# of them qualified; v1.2.2 removed them, so the filter is now a no-op guard.
intake_range <- intake_raw |>
  filter(qualified) |>
  summarise(
    min_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
stopifnot(as.Date(intake_range$max_date) == as.Date("2025-06-09"))

intake_range_sentence <- glue(
  "{format(intake_range$min_date, '%b %Y')} and {format(intake_range$max_date, '%b %Y')}"
)
```

## Data Source and Participants

The analyses reported here are part of a Stage 1 Registered Report [@ballou2024psychological], and the data collected for this study are part of the Open Play dataset [@ballou2025openplay, {v1.2.6}], a longitudinal dataset that combined multi-platform video game digital trace data with daily and biweekly psychological measures from adult gamers in the UK and US over a three-month period. Qualifying participants completed the intake survey between `r intake_range_sentence`. The digital trace data span the following periods: `r telemetry_range_sentence`.

This study received ethical approval from the Social Sciences and Humanities Inter-Divisional Research Ethics Committee at the University of Oxford (OII_CIA_23_107). All participants provided informed consent at the start of the study, including consent to their data being shared openly for reanalysis.

Participants were paid at an average rate of £12/hour, equating to £0.20 for a 1-minute screening, £2 for the 10-minute intake survey (plus £5 for linking at least one account with recent data), £0.80 for each 4-minute daily survey, and £2 for each 10-minute biweekly survey. Participants received a £10 bonus payment for completing at least 24 out of 30 daily surveys and/or 5 out of 6 biweekly surveys.

```{r}
#| label: build-demographics
#| include: false

# The analytic sample is defined by the models: all participants with a
# qualified intake record (Open Play v1.2.6) and at least one valid SWEMWBS
# response in biweekly waves 1-6. analytic_pids() (R/01_preprocess.R) is the
# single definition of this rule; load_survey_data() and every R/ script use
# it too. Telemetry-based playtime is zero for participants/waves without
# recorded play.
analysis_pids <- analytic_pids()

n_model <- length(analysis_pids)

# Participants of the earlier (v1.2.1) analytic sample removed by the rule
# (Data Source and Participants; Appendix A, Deviation D7). Written by
# R/00_revoked_pids.R, which compares the v1.2.1 and v1.2.6 intake files.
revoked_ref   <- read_csv(here("data/reference/revoked_qualified_pids.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)
no_intake_ref <- read_csv(here("data/reference/no_intake_record_pids.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)
n_revoked_intakes   <- nrow(revoked_ref)
n_revoked_in_sample <- sum(revoked_ref$in_v121_analytic_sample)
n_no_intake_v121    <- nrow(no_intake_ref)
# D7 context: of the revoked in-sample participants, how many never linked an
# account and how many have no console/PC telemetry at all; the no-intake group
# has no console/PC telemetry in the clean files by construction (data-process.qmd
# keeps only sessions of pids with an intake record; guarded).
n_revoked_never_linked <- sum(revoked_ref$in_v121_analytic_sample & !revoked_ref$linked_any)
n_revoked_no_telemetry <- sum(revoked_ref$in_v121_analytic_sample & !revoked_ref$any_telemetry)
stopifnot(n_revoked_never_linked > 0, n_revoked_no_telemetry >= n_revoked_never_linked,
          !any(no_intake_ref$any_telemetry))
stopifnot(
  n_revoked_in_sample == 133,
  !any(revoked_ref$pid %in% analysis_pids),
  !any(no_intake_ref$pid %in% analysis_pids)
)

genre_matched_pids <- read_csv(here("data/processed/genre_wave_long.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  pull(pid)

n_genre_matched <- length(intersect(analysis_pids, genre_matched_pids))

# Participants and person-waves in the analytic sample without any recorded
# Nintendo/Xbox/Steam play; they are retained with zero hours (sample
# paragraph). total_playtime.csv holds only person-waves with recorded play.
analysis_pw <- load_survey_data(analysis_pids) |>
  filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6, !is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  distinct(pid, wave)
played_pw <- read_csv(here("data/processed/total_playtime.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6, total_hours_per_day > 0) |>
  distinct(pid, wave)
# The processed telemetry outputs follow the same sample rule (waves are
# assigned only for analytic participants); a stale data/processed/ fails here.
stopifnot(
  setequal(unique(analysis_pw$pid), analysis_pids),
  all(played_pw$pid %in% analysis_pids),
  all(genre_matched_pids %in% analysis_pids)
)
n_waves_analytic  <- nrow(analysis_pw)
n_waves_zero_play <- nrow(anti_join(analysis_pw, played_pw, by = c("pid", "wave")))
n_pid_zero_play   <- sum(!(analysis_pids %in% played_pw$pid))

daily_telemetry <- bind_rows(
  read_csv(here("data/clean/xbox.csv.gz"),     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Xbox"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/steam.csv.gz"),    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Steam"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/nintendo.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Nintendo"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/ios.csv.gz"),      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "iOS"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/android.csv.gz"),  show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Android")
) |>
  distinct(pid, platform)

demographics <- intake |>
  filter(qualified) |>
  mutate(
    pid = as.character(pid),
    age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(17, 24, 30, 35, 40),
      labels = c("18-24", "25-30", "31-35", "36-40")
    ),
    gender = case_when(
      gender %in% c("Man", "Male")     ~ "Man",
      gender %in% c("Woman", "Female") ~ "Woman",
      gender == "Prefer not to say"    ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(gender)                    ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                             ~ "Non-binary/Other"
    ),
    ethnicity = case_when(
      ethnicity %in% c("White", "White alone")                                          ~ "White",
      ethnicity %in% c("Asian", "Asian alone", "Asian or Asian British")                ~ "Asian",
      ethnicity %in% c("Black", "Black or African American alone",
                       "Black, African, Caribbean or Black British")                    ~ "Black",
      ethnicity %in% c("Mixed", "Mixed or multiple ethnic groups", "Two or More Races") ~ "Mixed/Multiple",
      ethnicity == "Prefer not to say"                                                  ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(ethnicity)                                                                  ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                                                                              ~ "Other"
    )
  ) |>
  select(pid, country, age, age_group, gender, ethnicity)

analytic_sample <- demographics |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids, !is.na(age_group))

n_total <- nrow(analytic_sample)
n_us    <- sum(analytic_sample$country == "US", na.rm = TRUE)
n_uk    <- sum(analytic_sample$country == "UK", na.rm = TRUE)

n_intake_total <- nrow(intake)
n_qualified    <- sum(intake$qualified, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Of the `r txt_n_intake_total` participants who completed the intake survey, `r txt_n_qualified` met the preregistered screening and linking criteria. The analytic sample comprises the `r txt_n_model` qualified participants who provided valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly survey wave. This definition corrects the sample of our first analyses: a later Open Play release (v1.2.4) corrected false positives in the qualification flag, revoking it for participants whose intake had not passed the screening and linking checks, and we excluded them (`r txt_n_revoked_in_sample` participants of the earlier analytic sample), together with `r txt_n_no_intake_v121` participants whose biweekly responses carry a participant identifier that matches no intake record, an identifier mismatch in the data provider's survey export (Appendix A, Deviation D7; @tbl-frequentist-registered in Appendix D compares the preregistered estimates with and without them). We measured playtime for these participants from their linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam accounts. Rather than excluding participants and waves without recorded play on these platforms, we retained them with zero hours: `r txt_n_pid_zero_play` participants (`r txt_pct_pid_zero_play`%) had no recorded play in any wave, and `r txt_n_waves_zero_play` of the `r txt_n_waves_analytic` person-waves (`r txt_pct_waves_zero_play`%) had none in that wave. In the full analytic sample, `r txt_n_genre_matched` participants (`r txt_pct_genre_matched`%) had at least one session of a game that we could match to a genre. All `r txt_n_total` analytic-sample participants have an age within the 18-40 screening range (`r txt_n_us` US, `r txt_n_uk` UK; mean age `r txt_mean_age` years, `r txt_pct_men`% men), so the demographic sensitivity analysis starts from the full analytic sample. We report full demographic characteristics, including country-level breakdowns, in @tbl-demographics.

```{r}
#| label: genre-metadata-stats
#| include: false

# --- Raw IGDB label statistics (game_metadata.csv.gz) -----------------------
meta_raw_gm   <- read_csv(here("data/clean/game_metadata.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
meta_labelled <- meta_raw_gm |> filter(!is.na(genres), nchar(genres) > 0)
raw_label_list      <- map(str_split(meta_labelled$genres, ","), str_trim)
raw_labels_distinct <- sort(unique(unlist(raw_label_list)))
n_raw_genre_labels  <- length(raw_labels_distinct)
n_labels_per_game   <- lengths(raw_label_list)
max_raw_labels      <- max(n_labels_per_game)
pct_games_gt3_labels <- 100 * mean(n_labels_per_game > 3)

# Genre count under the PRE-REGISTERED collapsing (for Appendix B)
prereg_collapse <- function(g) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    g == "Hack and slash/Beat 'em up" ~ "Action",
    g %in% c("Turn-based strategy (TBS)", "Real Time Strategy (RTS)", "Tactical") ~ "Strategy",
    g %in% c("Point-and-click", "Visual Novel") ~ "Adventure",
    g == "Quiz/Trivia" ~ "Puzzle",
    TRUE ~ g
  )
}
n_prereg_genres <- n_distinct(prereg_collapse(raw_labels_distinct))

# --- Xbox genre coverage before/after the local mapping fix. Computed for
# reference only; the fix is ordinary data cleaning and is no longer reported
# in the text or catalogued as a deviation.
meta_fixed_gm <- populate_xbox_genres(meta_raw_gm)
xb_has <- function(meta) meta |> filter(platform == "Xbox") |>
  transmute(original_name, has = !is.na(genres) & nchar(genres) > 0)
xbox_cov <- telemetry_files$Xbox |>
  left_join(xb_has(meta_raw_gm),   by = c("title_id" = "original_name")) |>
  rename(has_before = has) |>
  left_join(xb_has(meta_fixed_gm), by = c("title_id" = "original_name")) |>
  rename(has_after = has) |>
  summarise(
    total_min  = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_before = sum(duration[replace_na(has_before, FALSE)], na.rm = TRUE),
    min_after  = sum(duration[replace_na(has_after,  FALSE)], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
xbox_pct_before  <- 100 * xbox_cov$min_before / xbox_cov$total_min
xbox_pct_after   <- 100 * xbox_cov$min_after  / xbox_cov$total_min
xbox_min_rescued <- xbox_cov$min_after - xbox_cov$min_before

# --- In-study (waves 1-6) sessions, from the already-loaded telemetry -------
survey_ms   <- load_survey_data() |> filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6)
sessions_ms <- bind_rows(
  telemetry_files$Nintendo |> transmute(pid, platform = "Nintendo", title_id, date, duration),
  telemetry_files$Xbox     |> transmute(pid, platform = "Xbox",     title_id, date, duration),
  telemetry_files$Steam    |> transmute(pid, platform = "Steam",    title_id, date, duration = minutes)
)
sessions_instudy <- add_waves(sessions_ms, survey_ms)

# Distinct in-study titles for the analytic sample (quoted in the abstract;
# pinned in abstract-claims-guard)
n_titles_instudy <- sessions_instudy |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  distinct(title_id, platform) |>
  nrow()

# Genre coverage of in-study playtime and platform composition (for Methods
# and Limitations): share of minutes matched to >= 1 study genre
matched_keys_ms <- load_game_metadata_long() |> distinct(original_name, platform)
cov_by_platform <- sessions_instudy |>
  left_join(matched_keys_ms |> mutate(matched = TRUE),
            by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  mutate(matched = replace_na(matched, FALSE)) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_matched = 100 * sum(duration[matched], na.rm = TRUE) / minutes,
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * minutes / sum(minutes))
genre_cov_overall <- with(cov_by_platform, 100 * sum(minutes * pct_matched / 100) / sum(minutes))
cov_get   <- function(p) cov_by_platform$pct_matched[cov_by_platform$platform == p]
share_get <- function(p) cov_by_platform$share[cov_by_platform$platform == p]

# --- Telemetry history depth and wave-1 behaviour/availability --------------
# All rates below use the analytic sample as their basis: play rates are
# per analytic-sample participant; availability is per analytic-sample
# participant with any telemetry on the platform.
first_dates_ms <- sessions_ms |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  group_by(pid, platform) |>
  summarise(first_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(survey_ms |> distinct(pid, baseline_date), by = "pid") |>
  mutate(days_before = as.numeric(baseline_date - first_date))
med_days <- first_dates_ms |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(median_days = median(days_before), .groups = "drop") |>
  (\(d) setNames(d$median_days, d$platform))()

w1_played <- sessions_instudy |>
  filter(wave == 1, pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  distinct(pid, platform)
w1_rate   <- function(p) 100 * sum(w1_played$platform == p) / n_model
# Availability: telemetry history covers the full wave-1 window
w1_avail <- first_dates_ms |>
  mutate(covers_w1 = days_before >= 14) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(covers_w1), .groups = "drop") |>
  (\(d) setNames(d$pct, d$platform))()

# Guard for the fixed prose: full-window telemetry availability is high on
# every platform among linked participants.
stopifnot(all(w1_avail[c("Nintendo", "Xbox", "Steam")] >= 80))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-mobile
#| include: false

survey <- load_survey_data()
# Waves with an incomplete SWEMWBS: they enter the person means of playtime
# (chunk model-data) but not the fits (Appendix F (M1)).
n_swemwbs_incomplete <- sum(is.na(survey$wemwbs))
stopifnot(n_swemwbs_incomplete > 0, n_swemwbs_incomplete < 500)
baselines <- survey |> distinct(pid, baseline_date)

ios     <- read_csv(here("data/clean/ios.csv.gz"),     show_col_types = FALSE)
android <- read_csv(here("data/clean/android.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)

mobile <- bind_rows(ios, android) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(day_local)) |>
  group_by(pid, date) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(baselines, by = "pid") |>
  filter(!is.na(baseline_date)) |>
  mutate(wave = assign_wave_vec(date, baseline_date)) |>
  filter(!is.na(wave), wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  group_by(pid, wave) |>
  summarise(mobile_hours_per_day = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE) / 60 / 14,
            .groups = "drop")

# Mobile minutes are joined to the survey frame (person-waves) in chunk
# build-aggregated-playtime, not to total_playtime: total_playtime holds only
# person-waves with console/PC play, so a join there dropped the mobile time
# of person-waves with mobile but no console/PC play (fixed 2026-10-13; the
# all-platform H1 model in chunk frequentist-registered joins the same way).
```

```{r}
#| label: build-aggregated-playtime
#| include: false

# Build wide-format aggregated_playtime and genre variable vectors from the
# new long-format pipeline (genre_wave_long + total_playtime + survey).
#
# Sanitize genre names to valid R column names, e.g.:
#   "Action & Adventure"  → "time_action_adventure"
#   "Role-playing (RPG)"  → "time_role_playing_rpg"
#   "Shooter"             → "time_shooter"
genre_to_col <- function(g) {
  col <- gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", tolower(g))
  col <- gsub("^_+|_+$", "", col)
  paste0("time_", col)
}

# Pivot genre_wave_long wide: one time_{genre} column per genre per pid × wave.
# values_fill = 0 handles genre × wave combos with no play.
genre_wide <- genre_wave_long |>
  mutate(col = genre_to_col(genre)) |>
  select(pid, wave, col, hours_per_day) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = hours_per_day, values_fill = 0)

genre_vars <- sort(setdiff(names(genre_wide), c("pid", "wave")))

# Build aggregated_playtime starting from the full survey (includes 0-play waves).
# Left-joining telemetry ensures participants who skipped gaming in a wave get 0.
# Console/PC playtime and mobile minutes are joined separately to the survey
# frame, so a person-wave with mobile but no console/PC play keeps its mobile
# time in the all-platform total (no double-counting: console/PC playtime
# comes from raw sessions via 01_preprocess.R).
aggregated_playtime <- survey |>
  select(pid, wave, wemwbs, self_reported_biweekly_play) |>
  left_join(
    total_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  left_join(mobile, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  left_join(genre_wide, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_genres    = replace_na(total_hours_per_day, 0),
    mobile_hours_per_day     = replace_na(mobile_hours_per_day, 0),
    total_time_all_platforms = total_time_all_genres + mobile_hours_per_day,
    across(all_of(genre_vars), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  select(-total_hours_per_day) |>
  # Within/between decompose over ALL survey waves (including 0-play waves)
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_platforms_within  =
      total_time_all_platforms - mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_time_all_platforms_between =
      mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(
      all_of(genre_vars),
      list(
        within  = ~ .x - mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        between = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

genre_within_vars  <- paste0(genre_vars, "_within")
genre_between_vars <- paste0(genre_vars, "_between")
genre_vars_demean  <- c(genre_within_vars, genre_between_vars)
```

```{r}
#| label: genre-descriptives-extended
#| include: false

# Map genre names to display format where needed
raw_to_display <- c(
  "Role-playing (RPG)"         = "Role-playing",
  "Hack and slash/Beat 'em up" = "Hack & Slash / Beat 'em Up",
  "Point-and-click"            = "Point-and-Click"
)

# Load metadata for display names (igdb_name preferred over original_name)
meta_display <- read_csv(here("data/clean/game_metadata.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(display_name = coalesce(igdb_name, original_name)) |>
  select(original_name, platform, display_name)

# Build session-level telemetry with genre + display name using current pipeline
meta_long_full <- load_game_metadata_long()
telemetry_genre <- load_genre_sessions(meta_long_full) |>
  add_waves(survey) |>
  left_join(meta_display, by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  mutate(
    display_name = coalesce(display_name, title_id),
    # Transliterate non-ASCII to avoid typst <label> parsing of encoded chars
    display_name = iconv(display_name, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"),
    genre_display = if_else(genre %in% names(raw_to_display),
                            unname(raw_to_display[genre]), genre)
  )

# Per-genre stats: n_games, total_minutes, mean_min_per_day, top 5 titles with % of genre playtime
total_person_days <- n_observations_total * 14

genre_stats <- telemetry_genre |>
  group_by(genre_display, title_id, display_name) |>
  summarise(total_min = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(genre_display) |>
  mutate(
    genre_total = sum(total_min),
    pct = round(100 * total_min / genre_total, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_min)) |>
  summarise(
    n_games = n(),
    total_minutes = first(genre_total),
    top_5 = paste(
      paste0(display_name[1:min(5, n())], " [", pct[1:min(5, n())], "%]"),
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    mean_min_per_day = first(genre_total) / total_person_days,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(genre = genre_display)

# Normalize genre_means labels for join
genre_means_norm <- genre_means |>
  mutate(genre = str_replace(genre, "^Role Playing Rpg\\s*$", "Role-playing"))

# Build extended descriptives table
genre_descriptives_extended <- genre_means_norm |>
  left_join(genre_stats, by = "genre") |>
  mutate(
    `n games` = replace_na(n_games, 0L),
    `Total hours` = round(replace_na(total_minutes, 0) / 60, 1),
    `Mean min/day` = round(replace_na(mean_min_per_day, 0), 1),
    `Top 5 titles` = replace_na(top_5, "")
  ) |>
  select(Genre = genre, `n games`, `Total hours`, `Mean min/day`, `Top 5 titles`)

# Total row
# Use total_playtime (computed from raw sessions, no multi-genre duplication)
# rather than summing telemetry_genre which counts multi-genre sessions multiple times.
total_minutes_all <- sum(total_playtime$total_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
total_row <- tibble(
  Genre = "Total (unique, deduplicated)",
  `n games` = n_distinct(telemetry_genre$title_id),
  `Total hours` = round(total_minutes_all / 60, 1),
  `Mean min/day` = round(mean_playtime * 60, 1),
  `Top 5 titles` = ""
)

genre_descriptives_extended <- bind_rows(genre_descriptives_extended, total_row)

# Shared 14-genre palette, ranked by in-study playtime: Okabe-Ito for the
# seven most-played genres, distinct extras for the rest. Purple is reserved
# for SWEMWBS. Reused by the descriptives figure and the co-occurrence figure
# (@fig-genre-upset).
genre_hours_tot <- telemetry_genre |>
  count(genre_display, wt = duration / 60, name = "hours") |>
  arrange(desc(hours))
rank14 <- genre_hours_tot$genre_display
okabe_ito <- c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73", "#56B4E9",
               "#CC79A7", "#D55E00", "#F0E442")
pal_genre <- setNames(
  c(okabe_ito, "#8B4513", "#117733", "#882255", "#44AA99",
    "#999933", "#DDCC77", "#5A5A5A"),
  rank14
)
stopifnot(length(rank14) == 14)

# Shared model palette: one colour per model family, used by the figure that
# encodes model with a legend (@fig-integrated-coefs). The posterior-row
# figures (@fig-h1-all-models, @fig-h2-heterogeneity, @fig-daily-posteriors)
# use a single fill because the row labels already name the model (MV, v4.1);
# the M1 entry and model_family() are kept for reuse.
model_palette <- c(
  "M1" = "#737373",
  "M2" = "#1f78b4",
  "M3" = "#ff8c00",
  "M4" = "#6a3d9a"
)
model_family <- function(x) sub("-D$", "", sub(":.*$", "", x))
```

## Measures

@fig-descriptives shows the distributions and structure of the key variables.

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-descriptives
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("*Distributions, Composition, and Raw Structure of the Study Measures.* (A) SWEMWBS distributions per biweekly wave (density and median box). (B) Average daily hours per person-wave with recorded play (15-minute bins; dashed line: median). (C) Share of recorded playtime per study day by platform, days 1\u201384. (D) Daily playtime for one participant (ID ", p75_pid, "); bar height is genre-matched playtime, segments are its genre composition under proportional multi-membership weighting. Dashed lines mark the six 14-day waves. Two outcomes are overlaid on the right axis: biweekly SWEMWBS (purple open squares, 1\u20135) at each survey date, and daily life satisfaction from the 30-day diary (red open circles, 0\u2013100).")'
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8.4
#| echo: false

desc_svy <- survey |> filter(pid %in% analysis_pids)

pw <- desc_svy |>
  select(pid, wave, wemwbs) |>
  left_join(total_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day),
            by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(total_hours_per_day = replace_na(total_hours_per_day, 0))
pct_zero_pw <- 100 * mean(pw$total_hours_per_day == 0)

# Panel A: SWEMWBS by wave (half-violin density + median box),
# fill lightening across waves 1-6.
panel_a <- desc_svy |>
  filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(wave), y = wemwbs, fill = factor(wave))) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.8, width = 0.6, justification = -0.25,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, fill = NA, colour = "grey20",
               linewidth = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("#5E3C99", "#D8CFEA"))(6),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 5)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(title = "Wellbeing by Wave", x = "Wave", y = "SWEMWBS (1\u20135)")

# Panel B: distribution of the playtime dose (15-minute bins; median marked)
pw_pos <- pw |> filter(total_hours_per_day > 0)
med_dose <- median(pw_pos$total_hours_per_day)
panel_b <- ggplot(pw_pos, aes(x = total_hours_per_day)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, fill = "#E69F00",
                 colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_dose, linetype = 2, colour = "grey20") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, quantile(pw_pos$total_hours_per_day, 0.99))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(title = "Playtime by Wave", x = "Average daily playtime (hours)", y = "Person-waves")

# Panel C: platform share of recorded playtime across study days
study_starts <- survey |>
  distinct(pid, baseline_date) |>
  filter(!is.na(baseline_date)) |>
  transmute(pid, study_start = as.Date(baseline_date))

plat_daily <- bind_rows(
  telemetry_files$Nintendo |> transmute(pid, date, platform = "Nintendo", minutes = duration),
  telemetry_files$Xbox     |> transmute(pid, date, platform = "Xbox",     minutes = duration),
  telemetry_files$Steam    |> transmute(pid, date, platform = "Steam",    minutes = minutes)
) |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
  mutate(study_day = as.integer(date - study_start) + 1L) |>
  filter(study_day >= 1, study_day <= 84) |>
  count(study_day, platform, wt = minutes, name = "minutes") |>
  group_by(study_day) |>
  mutate(prop = minutes / sum(minutes)) |>
  ungroup()

panel_c <- ggplot(plat_daily, aes(x = study_day, y = prop, fill = platform)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Nintendo = "#D55E00", Steam = "#0072B2", Xbox = "#009E73")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 84, 14)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(title = "Platform Composition", x = "Study day", y = "Share of playtime", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 12.5))

# Panel D: one participant (75th percentile of playtime), day by day, with
# each day represented the way M4 represents a wave: bar height = clock time
# of genre-matched play, segments = w_g * total, where w_g = full-attribution
# genre minutes / their sum (proportional multi-membership weighting,
# Methods). Days are counted from baseline (day 0); waves 1-6 are the 14-day
# blocks ending on the survey days (days -14..69), marked by dashed lines.
daily_genre_telemetry <- load_genre_sessions(meta_long_full) |>
  group_by(pid, platform, title_id, date) |>
  mutate(n_labels = n_distinct(genre)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(pid, date, genre) |>
  summarise(minutes_full  = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
            minutes_clock = sum(duration / n_labels, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(day_local = date) |>
  mutate(genre_display = if_else(genre %in% names(raw_to_display),
                                 unname(raw_to_display[genre]), genre))

dgs <- daily_genre_telemetry |>
  inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
  mutate(study_day = as.integer(day_local - study_start)) |>
  filter(study_day >= -14, study_day <= 69)

eligible_cs <- desc_svy |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(n_surveys = sum(!is.na(wemwbs)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_surveys >= 3)

tot_by_pid <- dgs |>
  semi_join(eligible_cs, by = "pid") |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(total_minutes = sum(minutes_clock),
            n_genres = n_distinct(genre), .groups = "drop")

# Shown participant: chosen for informativeness (recorded play in every wave,
# many genres, both outcomes observed). p_show_pct records where they sit in
# the distribution of genre-matched playtime (no longer quoted in the caption).
p75_pid <- "p5271179686"
stopifnot(p75_pid %in% tot_by_pid$pid, p75_pid %in% analysis_pids)
p_show_pct <- round(100 * mean(tot_by_pid$total_minutes <=
                                 tot_by_pid$total_minutes[tot_by_pid$pid == p75_pid]))

# Daily diary (life satisfaction 0-100; completion is UTC, utc_offset in hours)
daily_lite <- read_csv(here("data/processed/daily/daily_model_frame.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(pid, completion, utc_offset, life_sat)

outcome_cols <- c(wb = "#5E3C99", ls = "#C1272D")
outcome_labs <- c(wb = "SWEMWBS", ls = "Daily life satisfaction")
wave_edges   <- seq(-14.5, 69.5, by = 14)

# Panel D builder: one participant, days -14..69 from baseline, bars = clock
# time of genre-matched play composed with M4's proportional weights, SWEMWBS
# and daily life satisfaction overlaid on a shared right axis (0-100 mapped
# linearly onto 1-5). Legend lists only the genres this participant played.
make_panel_d <- function(pid_sel, title = "One Participant in Full") {
  cs_day <- dgs |>
    filter(pid == pid_sel) |>
    group_by(study_day) |>
    mutate(total_clock = sum(minutes_clock),
           w = minutes_full / sum(minutes_full)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    transmute(study_day, g = genre_display, w, minutes = w * total_clock)

  cs_grid <- expand_grid(study_day = -14:69, g = rank14) |>
    left_join(cs_day, by = c("study_day", "g")) |>
    mutate(w = replace_na(w, 0), minutes = replace_na(minutes, 0),
           g = factor(g, levels = rank14))

  # Guards: shares sum to 1 on every day with play; stacked bars are clock time
  w_check <- cs_grid |> group_by(study_day) |> summarise(w = sum(w), m = sum(minutes))
  stopifnot(all(abs(w_check$w[w_check$w > 0] - 1) < 1e-6), max(w_check$m) <= 24 * 60)
  played <- cs_grid |> group_by(g) |> summarise(m = sum(minutes)) |>
    filter(m > 0) |> pull(g) |> as.character()

  # Biweekly survey timestamps are UTC; convert to the participant's local date
  # using their modal UTC offset from the daily diary (0 if not in the diary).
  cs_offset <- daily_lite |> filter(pid == pid_sel) |>
    count(utc_offset, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 1) |> pull(utc_offset)
  if (length(cs_offset) == 0) cs_offset <- 0
  cs_wb <- desc_svy |>
    filter(pid == pid_sel, !is.na(wemwbs)) |>
    inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
    mutate(local_date = as.Date(as.POSIXct(date, tz = "UTC") + cs_offset * 3600, tz = "UTC"),
           study_day  = as.integer(local_date - study_start)) |>
    select(study_day, wemwbs)
  cs_daily <- daily_lite |>
    filter(pid == pid_sel, !is.na(life_sat)) |>
    inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
    mutate(local_date = as.Date(completion + utc_offset * 3600, tz = "UTC"),
           study_day  = as.integer(local_date - study_start)) |>
    filter(study_day >= -14, study_day <= 69) |>
    select(study_day, life_sat)

  coeff_cs <- max(w_check$m) / 4
  x_max_d  <- max(70.5, max(cs_wb$study_day, -Inf) + 0.5)
  x_scale_d <- scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-14.5, x_max_d), breaks = seq(-14, 70, 14),
                                  expand = c(0.01, 0))

  ggplot() +
    geom_col(data = cs_grid, aes(x = study_day, y = minutes, fill = g), width = 1) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = wave_edges, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
    annotate("text", x = wave_edges[-7] + 7, y = max(w_check$m) * 1.04,
             label = paste("Wave", 1:6), size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_line(data = cs_daily,
              aes(x = study_day, y = life_sat / 25 * coeff_cs, colour = "ls"),
              linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = cs_daily,
               aes(x = study_day, y = life_sat / 25 * coeff_cs, colour = "ls", shape = "ls"),
               fill = "white", size = 2.1, stroke = 0.9) +
    geom_line(data = cs_wb,
              aes(x = study_day, y = (wemwbs - 1) * coeff_cs, colour = "wb"),
              linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_point(data = cs_wb,
               aes(x = study_day, y = (wemwbs - 1) * coeff_cs, colour = "wb", shape = "wb"),
               fill = "white", size = 2.6, stroke = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = outcome_cols, labels = outcome_labs, name = NULL,
                        limits = c("wb", "ls"), drop = FALSE) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(wb = 22, ls = 21), labels = outcome_labs, name = NULL,
                       limits = c("wb", "ls"), drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal_genre, name = NULL, breaks = played) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1, ncol = 1,
                                 override.aes = list(shape = c(22, 21), fill = "white",
                                                     size = c(2.6, 2.1), linewidth = c(1.1, 0.7))),
           shape  = "none",
           fill   = guide_legend(nrow = 2, order = 2)) +
    x_scale_d +
    scale_y_continuous(
      "Daily playtime (minutes)",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / coeff_cs + 1,
                          name = sprintf("<span style='color:%s'>SWEMWBS</span>  |  <span style='color:%s'>Daily life satisfaction</span>",
                                         outcome_cols[["wb"]], outcome_cols[["ls"]]),
                          breaks = 1:5,
                          labels = function(b) sprintf(
                            "<span style='color:%s'>%s</span> | <span style='color:%s'>%s</span>",
                            outcome_cols[["wb"]], b, outcome_cols[["ls"]], (b - 1) * 25))
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Days from baseline", tag = "D") +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal",
      legend.box.just = "top",
      legend.key.size = unit(4, "mm"), legend.key.spacing.x = unit(3, "mm"),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
      legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), legend.spacing.x = unit(2, "mm"),
      axis.title.y.right = ggtext::element_markdown(angle = 90),
      axis.text.y.right  = ggtext::element_markdown(),
      axis.ticks.y.right = element_line(colour = "grey40")
    )
}

panel_d <- make_panel_d(p75_pid)

p_descriptives <- ((panel_a + labs(tag = "A") | panel_b + labs(tag = "B") |
                    panel_c + labs(tag = "C")) / panel_d) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.15)) &
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.tag = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 4)),
        plot.margin = margin(4, 6, 2, 4))

p_descriptives
```

```{r}
#| label: swemwbs-reliability
#| include: false

# Internal consistency of the 7 SWEMWBS items over all analytic person-waves
# (McDonald's omega total and Cronbach's alpha; psych). Reported in Measures.
swemwbs_items <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_biweekly.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids, wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  select(starts_with("wemwbs_")) |>
  drop_na()
stopifnot(ncol(swemwbs_items) == 7)
swemwbs_omega <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::omega(swemwbs_items, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)))$omega.tot
swemwbs_alpha <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(psych::alpha(swemwbs_items)))$total$raw_alpha
stopifnot(swemwbs_omega > 0.8, swemwbs_alpha > 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| label: txt-measures-1
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_swemwbs_omega <- sprintf("%.2f", swemwbs_omega)
txt_swemwbs_alpha <- sprintf("%.2f", swemwbs_alpha)
```

**Wellbeing.** We assessed wellbeing with the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (SWEMWBS) [@tennant2007warwick], a 7-item short form of the WEMWBS covering psychological functioning and subjective wellbeing over the past 2 weeks, with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "None of the time" to "All of the time." We score the scale as the arithmetic mean of the 7 items (range: 1–5). Internal consistency across all analytic person-waves was high (McDonald's ω~t~ = `r txt_swemwbs_omega`, Cronbach's α = `r txt_swemwbs_alpha`). We define all reported coefficients, the priors, and the preregistered SESOI on this item-mean scale.

**Video game playtime.** Digital trace data from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam provide session-level records (per-title start and end timestamps), while iOS and Android contribute only daily aggregate minutes (no game-level metadata). Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam therefore contribute to both H1 (total playtime) and H2 (genre-specific playtime); iOS and Android enter only the first positive control, which compares self-reported with logged playtime, and the preregistered all-platform H1 model, which Appendix D reports with the other preregistered frequentist analyses (@tbl-frequentist-registered; Appendix A, Deviation D4). Our findings therefore concern play on Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam and do not speak to mobile play.

```{r}
#| label: genre-upset-data
#| include: false

# Filter to only games played by participants in the analysis.
# telemetry_genre (loaded above) contains wave-assigned sessions for study
# participants; semi_join restricts meta_long_full to those title_ids only.
relevant_games <- telemetry_genre |> distinct(title_id, platform)

# Build combination labels and playtime per game-platform pair
game_combos <- meta_long_full |>
  semi_join(relevant_games, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  distinct(original_name, platform, genre) |>
  group_by(original_name, platform) |>
  summarise(combination = paste(sort(genre), collapse = " + "), .groups = "drop")

n_total_games <- nrow(game_combos)

# Total playtime per game-platform pair.
# telemetry_genre is genre-long (one row per session x genre label), so a
# k-genre game's sessions appear k times; divide by the game's label count
# to recover true playtime. Within a game the label set is constant.
game_hours <- telemetry_genre |>
  group_by(title_id, platform) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE) / 60 / n_distinct(genre),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Summary statistics for the co-occurrence prose in Measures
cooc_stats <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(
    total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0),
    multi = str_detect(combination, fixed(" + "))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_combinations       = n_distinct(combination),
    pct_multigenre_games = 100 * mean(multi),
    pct_multigenre_hours = 100 * sum(total_hours[multi]) / sum(total_hours)
  )
n_combinations       <- cooc_stats$n_combinations
pct_multigenre_games <- cooc_stats$pct_multigenre_games
pct_multigenre_hours <- cooc_stats$pct_multigenre_hours

# --- Data for playtime-weighted UpSet plot (exact hours) ---
# Hours per genre combination over all games (denominator for the top-40 share)
combo_hours_all <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0)) |>
  group_by(combination) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(total_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(hours))

int_hours <- combo_hours_all |>
  slice_head(n = 40) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number())

# Share of all genre-matched playtime covered by the 40 plotted combinations
pct_top40_hours <- 100 * sum(int_hours$hours) / sum(combo_hours_all$hours)
stopifnot(pct_top40_hours > 0, pct_top40_hours <= 100)

# Parse each combination into its constituent genres
int_genres <- int_hours |>
  mutate(genres_list = str_split(combination, " \\+ ")) |>
  unnest(genres_list) |>
  rename(genre = genres_list)

# All genres appearing in the top intersections (ordered by total hours across
# all games, ascending so the most common genre appears at the top of the matrix)
genre_totals <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0)) |>
  mutate(genres_list = str_split(combination, " \\+ ")) |>
  unnest(genres_list) |>
  group_by(genre = genres_list) |>
  summarise(genre_hours = sum(total_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(genre_hours)

genre_order <- genre_totals$genre

# Dot matrix: which genres are active for each intersection
dot_df <- expand_grid(rank = int_hours$rank, genre = genre_order) |>
  left_join(int_genres |> select(rank, genre) |> mutate(active = TRUE),
            by = c("rank", "genre")) |>
  mutate(active = replace_na(active, FALSE),
         genre = factor(genre, levels = genre_order))

# Connecting segments between active dots in multi-genre intersections
seg_df <- int_genres |>
  mutate(ypos = match(genre, genre_order)) |>
  group_by(rank) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(
    ymin = genre_order[min(ypos)],
    ymax = genre_order[max(ypos)],
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: txt-measures-2
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_genre_cov_overall <- round(genre_cov_overall, 1)
txt_cov_get_Steam <- round(cov_get("Steam"), 1)
txt_cov_get_Nintendo <- round(cov_get("Nintendo"), 1)
txt_cov_get_Xbox <- round(cov_get("Xbox"), 1)
txt_n_total_games <- formatC(n_total_games, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
txt_pct_multigenre_games <- round(pct_multigenre_games)
txt_pct_top40_hours <- round(pct_top40_hours)
# The prose says 'a majority of games' / 'most games' carry several labels
stopifnot(pct_multigenre_games > 50)
```

**Game genre classification.** We obtained genre labels for Nintendo and Steam games by cross-referencing the game titles in the digital trace data with the Internet Games Database (IGDB). IGDB is, to our knowledge, the only database with complete multi-platform metadata coverage that offers an API for programmatic data retrieval. IGDB crowd-sources its genre labels from a predefined list of options: community members submit contributions (e.g., a new game or an alternative categorisation), which administrators and moderators vet before they appear in the database; IGDB documents its contribution guidelines publicly, including how it holds submissions for review and the predefined list of genres (<https://github.com/twitchtv/igdb-contribution-guidelines/wiki>). We could not match Xbox titles to IGDB, because Xbox provided us only with anonymised title identifiers; instead, we took the genre labels that Xbox supplies for each title through its store and mapped those onto the IGDB taxonomy. In total, we collected `r n_raw_genre_labels` distinct raw IGDB genre labels, converted the Xbox store genres into the IGDB taxonomy, and collapsed them into 14 genre categories (e.g., Strategy subsumes Turn-Based Strategy (TBS), Real-Time Strategy (RTS), Tactical, and MOBA; Puzzle subsumes Card & Board Game and Quiz/Trivia). Appendix B gives the complete mapping table, including where the implemented collapsing departs from the preregistered one (Deviation D2), and Appendix C the descriptive statistics by genre. We did not consider IGDB "themes" or other metadata fields. Overall, we matched `r txt_genre_cov_overall`% of in-study playtime to at least one study genre (Steam `r txt_cov_get_Steam`%, Nintendo `r txt_cov_get_Nintendo`%, Xbox `r txt_cov_get_Xbox`%); unmatched playtime counts towards total playtime but towards no genre.

**Genre co-occurrence and compositional multi-genre attribution.** Across the `r txt_n_total_games` individual games in our dataset, `r txt_pct_multigenre_games`% carry more than one genre label, leading to `r n_combinations` distinct genre combinations. @fig-genre-upset shows the playtime-weighted co-occurrence structure across the 40 most-played combinations, which together account for `r txt_pct_top40_hours`% of all genre-matched playtime, and @tbl-genre-cooccurrence lists the ten most-played combinations with their top titles. Because a majority of games carry several labels, the rule that turns a session of a multi-genre game into genre exposure variables decides what a genre coefficient means, so we set out the four rules we considered and the choices we made before describing the models. The preregistration specified the first; the confirmatory model M2 and the exploratory model M3 use the third (Appendix A, Deviation D1); and the exploratory model M4 uses the fourth.

*Primary attribution*, the preregistered rule, assigns each game to the genre that IGDB lists first and counts a session's full duration towards that genre alone. A 60-minute session of *Skyrim* (Adventure and RPG) would count as 60 minutes of whichever of its two genres IGDB happens to list first and nothing towards the other. Genre exposures then stay mutually exclusive and sum to total playtime, but the rule discards the second and third labels of most games and makes the exposure depend on the order in which IGDB lists them. After data access and before any results were known, we decided not to use it (Deviation D1).

*Partial attribution* splits a session's playtime across its genres. A 60-minute session of *Skyrim* (Adventure and RPG) would contribute 30 minutes to Adventure and 30 minutes to RPG (or potentially a different, unequal partition). Exposures then still sum to total playtime, but the rule penalises multi-genre games: each additional label a game carries lowers its contribution to every genre, although the game belongs fully to each of its genres rather than partially. We rejected this rule for that reason.

*Full attribution*, which we used for M2 and M3, counts a session's full duration towards every genre it carries. The same 60-minute *Skyrim* session counts as 60 minutes of Adventure and 60 minutes of RPG. Consider a person who plays 60 minutes of *Skyrim* (Adventure + RPG) and 60 minutes of *Final Fantasy XIV Online* (RPG only). Under partial attribution, *Skyrim* contributes 30 minutes to each genre, yielding 30 total minutes of Adventure and 90 minutes of RPG, a 1:3 ratio implying three times as much RPG engagement as Adventure. Under full attribution, *Skyrim* contributes 60 minutes to each genre, yielding 60 minutes of Adventure and 120 minutes of RPG, a 2:1 ratio that better reflects that RPG-labelled content received twice the engagement of Adventure-labelled content. A consequence is that genre exposures no longer sum to total playtime. Genre-level coefficients therefore represent the association with an added hour of that genre's exposure holding total playtime constant, for example, replacing a single-genre RPG session with a dual-genre Adventure/RPG session of the same length.

*Proportional multi-membership weighting*, which we used for M4, converts the full-attribution hours into compositional weights by dividing each genre's exposure hours by total exposure (e.g., 33.3% Adventure, 66.7% RPG for a wave consisting of 60 minutes of *Skyrim* and 60 minutes of *Final Fantasy XIV Online*) and uses these as the weights of a multiple-membership structure [@fielding2006cross; @cafri2015introduction] on a single total-playtime slope. Genre does not enter M4 as an independent predictor of wellbeing but as a modifier of the playtime–wellbeing slope: a wave consisting mostly of RPG play has its playtime coefficient adjusted mostly by the RPG slope adjustment, with other genres contributing in proportion to their share of that wave's play. M4 draws the genre-specific slope adjustments from a common distribution, and the standard deviation of that distribution, σ~s~, describes the genre differences that H2 concerns. This weighting shares a limitation with partial attribution, because adding a genre label to a game lowers the shares of the labels it already carries, so none of the four rules is free of trade-offs. In sum, M2 and M3 model full-attribution exposures, M4 models the same hours as proportional weights, and no model in the main text uses the preregistered primary attribution (Appendix D reports the preregistered tests under it), so every genre coefficient below describes exposure to games carrying a label rather than to games filed under it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-genre-upset
#| fig-cap: "*Genre Co-Occurrence Weighted by Total Playtime.* Top panel: total hours played by games in each genre combination, ordered by playtime. Bottom panel: dot matrix indicating which genres belong to each combination; connected dots denote multi-genre games. Left bars show total hours attributed to each genre, counting a multi-genre game's full playtime towards each genre exposure."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false

# Shared 14-genre palette (pal_genre, keyed on display names) applied to the
# genre bars and matrix dots; map this figure's raw genre names to display.
col_for_genre <- function(g) {
  disp <- ifelse(g %in% names(raw_to_display), unname(raw_to_display[g]), g)
  unname(pal_genre[disp])
}
stopifnot(!any(is.na(col_for_genre(as.character(genre_totals$genre)))))

# Top panel: bar chart of exact hours per intersection
p_bars <- ggplot(int_hours, aes(x = rank, y = hours)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey30", width = 0.35) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = int_hours$rank, expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  labs(y = "Total hours played") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x  = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    plot.margin  = margin(2, 5, 0, 5)
  )

# Bottom panel: dot-and-line matrix. Layer order is bottom to top: segments,
# inactive dots, active dots, so every dot sits on top of the connecting line;
# shape 21 with a white outline makes the break visible at any resolution.
dot_plot_df <- dot_df |>
  mutate(colour_key = ifelse(active, as.character(genre), "inactive"))

p_matrix <- ggplot(dot_plot_df, aes(x = rank, y = genre)) +
  geom_segment(data = seg_df,
               aes(x = rank, xend = rank, y = ymin, yend = ymax),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(data = dot_plot_df |> filter(!active),
             shape = 21, fill = "grey85", colour = "white", stroke = 0.4, size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = dot_plot_df |> filter(active),
             aes(fill = colour_key), shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.4,
             size = 2.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(col_for_genre(unique(as.character(dot_df$genre))),
                                      unique(as.character(dot_df$genre)))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = int_hours$rank, expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  labs(y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x  = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    panel.grid   = element_blank(),
    plot.margin  = margin(0, 5, 2, 5)
  )

# Left panel: genre totals (horizontal bars), shared 14-genre palette
p_genre <- ggplot(genre_totals |> mutate(genre = factor(genre, levels = genre_order)),
                  aes(x = genre_hours, y = genre, fill = genre)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(col_for_genre(as.character(genre_totals$genre)),
                                      as.character(genre_totals$genre)),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_reverse(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right") +
  labs(x = "Hours per genre") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    plot.margin  = margin(0, 0, 2, 5)
  )

# Compose: left genre bars aligned with the dot matrix; bars on top
# Use patchwork: flat 2x2 grid so columns align across rows
p_spacer <- plot_spacer()

p_spacer + p_bars + p_genre + p_matrix +
  plot_layout(
    design = "AB\nCD",
    heights = c(3, 2),
    widths  = c(1, 4)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-genre-cooccurrence
#| tbl-cap: "Top 10 genre combinations by total playtime. Multi-genre rows join labels with ' + '. Total hours = playtime for games with that combination; % of playtime = share of all genre-matched playtime; n games = unique game-platform pairs. Xbox titles are anonymised (and truncated for this table)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| echo: false

# Session-level stats per combination.
# telemetry_genre already has display_name from the genre-descriptives-extended chunk.
# Deflate genre-long rows by each game's label count (see game_hours above)
# so per-title minutes count each session once.
title_min <- telemetry_genre |>
  left_join(game_combos, by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  filter(!is.na(combination)) |>
  # Anonymised Xbox title ids are UUIDs; show only their first eight characters so the
  # Top 5 column fits (the caption notes the truncation). title_id stays in
  # the grouping, so truncated ids never merge distinct games.
  mutate(display_name = str_replace(
    display_name,
    "^([0-9A-Fa-f]{8})-[0-9A-Fa-f]{4}-[0-9A-Fa-f]{4}-[0-9A-Fa-f]{4}-[0-9A-Fa-f]{12}$",
    "\\1…"
  )) |>
  group_by(combination, title_id, display_name) |>
  summarise(total_min = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE) / n_distinct(genre),
            .groups = "drop")

total_matched_minutes <- sum(title_min$total_min)

combo_stats <- title_min |>
  group_by(combination) |>
  mutate(
    combo_total = sum(total_min),
    pct_title   = round(100 * total_min / combo_total, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_min)) |>
  summarise(
    n_games          = n(),
    total_minutes    = first(combo_total),
    mean_min_per_day = first(combo_total) / total_person_days,
    top_5 = paste(
      paste0(display_name[1:min(5, n())], " [", pct_title[1:min(5, n())], "%]"),
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_minutes)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    `% of playtime` = round(100 * total_minutes / total_matched_minutes, 1)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    `Genre (or combination)` = gsub("[()]", "", gsub("Role-playing (RPG)", "Role-playing", combination, fixed = TRUE)),
    `Total hours`       = round(total_minutes / 60, 1),
    `% of playtime`,
    `n games`           = n_games,
    `Mean min/day`      = round(mean_min_per_day, 1),
    `Top 5 titles`      = replace_na(top_5, "")
  )

combo_stats |>
  tt(width = c(0.20, 0.09, 0.10, 0.08, 0.09, 0.44)) |>
  format_tt(digits = 1) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```
