Continued debate about how different games might differ in their effects on wellbeing persists in part because of measurement challenges, whereby prior genre research has been subject to at least one of three limitations, and usually multiple. First, genre assignment is inconsistent and unreliable: labels are typically self-assigned by participants or researchers, the same games are classified into different genres across studies, and nearly all taxonomies force each game into a single genre despite modern games being multi-genre by design [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @kingMaladaptivePlayergameRelationships2019]. Second, playtime has often been self-reported rather than logged, yet self-reported and logged media use correlate only moderately, with a meta-analytic estimate of *r* = 0.38 and fewer than one in ten self-reports falling within 5% of the logged value [@parrySystematicReviewMetaanalysis2021]. Our own positive control, which compared self-reported biweekly playtime with the logged total, gave *r* = `r txt_dqc1_result_estimate`: somewhat above the meta-analytic value, but still a correlation at which self-reports share only `r txt_dqc1_r2_pct`% of their variance with logged play, and one that may be depressed because the self-reports can also cover play on platforms outside our telemetry. Self-report and telemetry therefore agree on who plays more and who plays less, but too loosely to stand in for one another. Third, studies often cover a single game or a handful of titles [@bruhlmannMotivationalProfilingLeague2020; @JohannesEtAl2021video; @larrieuHowGamingMotives2023], leaving genre contrasts to be assembled across different studies that classified and measured both play and genre incommensurably, and often years apart in a medium whose genre labels drift as it evolves [@cohenHistoryGenre1986; @vargas-iglesiasMakingSenseGenre2020], so that a label such as adventure need not have covered the same games in each.

This study represents an advancement on all three fronts. Genre labels follow a single crowd-sourced taxonomy applied uniformly to every title across all platforms, retaining multiple genre labels where relevant. Playtime is measured as objective session-level telemetry across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam rather than self-reported. And all 14 genres are estimated jointly within a single sample, so genre contrasts emerge from one dataset with a common measurement of play, genre, and wellbeing.

## The playtime-wellbeing association is practically equivalent to zero

When participants played more than their own average in a given two-week wave, their wellbeing barely changed, consistent with previous digital trace studies that have repeatedly found aggregate playtime to be a poor predictor of wellbeing fluctuations [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025; @larrieuHowGamingMotives2023]. Between participants, practical equivalence was likewise established.

Inverting the estimates shows what these associations would amount to even if they were causal. Within persons, wellbeing would shift by one minimally important difference only after roughly `r txt_hours_to_mid_within` additional hours of play per day at the point estimate, and after `r txt_hours_to_mid_within_bound` additional hours at the credible bound most favourable to an association, more extreme than the 10 additional daily hours that @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022 derived from game-level telemetry. Between participants, the habitual difference needed to reach the same threshold lies between `r txt_hours_to_mid_between_bound` and `r txt_hours_to_mid_between` hours of daily play. Both requirements exceed the roughly five hours of leisure that US adults have in a day [@sturmFreeTimePhysical2019], and changes of this order do not occur in practice: of the `r txt_n_swing_pids` participants observed across adjacent waves, only `r n_swing4` ever changed their average daily play by 4 or more hours from one wave to the next. An association that no achievable play exposure can reach is, for every practical purpose, indistinguishable from no association at all.

The contrast between light and heavy players deserves one further remark. Participants who habitually play more reported slightly lower average wellbeing, yet the same participants' wellbeing did not fall in waves when they played more than usual. This within-null, between-negative pattern recurs across observational media research and is most plausibly a selection effect, in which people with lower baseline wellbeing spend more time in games rather than games lowering wellbeing [@robinson1950ecological; @kievit2013simpsons; @rohrer2023within; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025], although a cumulative effect accruing over years would look the same at these timescales [cf. @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022]. Whichever explanation holds, the difference is too small to matter, so public claims about gamers' mental health are, in effect, reports about who plays, not about what playing does.

The causal estimates from Japanese console lotteries point the other way, at 0.2 to 0.5 standard deviations per additional daily hour among lottery winners who acquired a console because they won [@egami2024causal; @egamiCausalEffectVideo2026]. Those are local effects of acquiring a new console, measured with self-reported play over the preceding month and diminishing at longer play durations, whereas our within-person estimates describe logged deviations from each person's usual playtime among people who already play. The two estimands need not agree: gaining access to a console and playing an extra hour on a console one already owns are different versions of the same nominal exposure [@magnusson2024harmful].

## Associations are close to zero in every genre

We expected genres to differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing. The preregistered joint test supports this prediction within persons, where the 14 genre coefficients are not all equal, but not between persons, and under the preregistered primary-genre attribution neither test rejects equality (Appendix D). The differences it detects lie between genre effects that are all close to zero: under the hierarchical prior, the 14 within-person genre estimates span only `r txt_m3_within_min` to `r txt_m3_within_max`, with no estimate more than a third of the SESOI from zero, and the most-played genres by total playtime (`r txt_top4_genres`; see @fig-genre-upset) sit inside this same narrow band. The spread estimated by the same model implies an expected `r txt_tau_share_n_genres` of the 14 genres more than 0.06 from the average genre effect and `r txt_tau_pair_mean_pct`% of genre pairs more than 0.06 apart, and on average `r txt_tau_rope_out_mean_pct`% of its within-person and `r txt_tau_rope_out_b_mean_pct`% of its between-person genre-effect distribution lie outside the ROPE. The multi-membership model is less precise than the hierarchical prior model: its fitted spread implies that about `r txt_sigma_sw_share_mean_pct0`% of genres (95% CI \[`r txt_sigma_sw_share_ci_lo_pct0`%, `r txt_sigma_sw_share_ci_hi_pct0`%\]) deviate from the average slope by more than 0.06, an expected `r txt_sigma_sw_share_n_hi` of the 14 genres at the upper credible bound, so differences confined to a few genres cannot be excluded. Inference about single genres is limited as well, because the credible intervals for rarely played genres remain wide: under the preregistered model, the widest within-person interval (`r m2_widest_genre`) is about `r txt_m2_width_ratio` times wider than the narrowest. Genres were statistically distinguishable only within persons and only when each game counted towards all its genres, and under the hierarchical prior no genre's estimated association approached the SESOI; any defence of playtime nulls that appeals to the heterogeneous nature of video games must look to partitions finer than genre.

This result does not contradict the genre differences reported before, because those concern other outcomes and other designs. The most consistent findings involve gaming disorder symptoms, where MMORPG, shooter, and strategy play stand out in cross-sectional surveys of self-reported genre preference [@elliottContributionGameGenre2012; @naInfluenceGameGenre2017; @kingMaladaptivePlayergameRelationships2019; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021], and player experience, where genres differ in immersion, autonomy, and frustration [@johnsonAllThatBase2015a; @hazelExploringPossibleMental2022]. Genre also explains little of why people play: among more than 14,000 highly engaged players, correlations between six gaming motives and genre preference ranged from −0.25 to 0.20 [@kiralyComprehensiveModelUnderstand2022]. Our estimand, the association between logged exposure to a genre and general wellbeing, is different, and on that estimand every genre's association lies close to zero.

## A Susceptible Minority Is Possible but Small

Still, a null average could conceal a minority for whom play, in total or in specific genres, genuinely matters [cf. @karhulahti2025claims]. The random slope in M1 addresses the total-playtime case by modelling each participant's own within-person association between playtime and wellbeing. The relevant quantity is the share of participants the model implies lie beyond the SESOI: combining the posterior for the average within-person effect with the posterior for the person-level slope standard deviation (`r txt_sd_slope_mean`, 95% CI \[`r txt_sd_slope_ci_lo`, `r txt_sd_slope_ci_hi`\]) under the model's normality assumption, an estimated `r txt_prop_mean_pct`% of participants (95% CI \[`r txt_prop_ci_lo_pct`%, `r txt_prop_ci_hi_pct`%\]) have a true within-person association exceeding 0.06 SWEMWBS points per daily hour in either direction. A susceptible minority is therefore entirely compatible with our results; what the data constrain is that such susceptibility is neither common nor, for most of the distribution, large at these timescales. Person-specific slope estimates are heavily shrunk towards the mean given the number of waves per participant, so the model quantifies how heavy the tails are without being able to identify which individuals occupy them; targeted designs with denser within-person sampling would be needed for that.

## Shortening the Window Does Not Recover an Effect

A further possibility is temporal, namely that the wellbeing effects of play might surface and dissipate faster than a biweekly retrospective survey can register. To test this claim, the exploratory daily analysis shortens the window from fourteen days to one and reproduces the total-playtime conclusion. Within persons, every total-playtime estimate lies inside the equivalence region under every specification, and the same-day point estimate is positive, roughly double its biweekly counterpart in within-person standard-deviation units (`r txt_d_b1_sd_units` versus `r txt_beta1_sd_units` s~w~ per hour). The direction is consistent with the session-level affective uplift reported among *PowerWash Simulator* players [@vuorreAffectiveUpliftVideo2024], though its resolution is fragile across the robustness refits and should be read as suggestive. Its practical magnitude is negligible either way: shifting daily life satisfaction by one minimally important difference (`r d_mid_daily` points on the 0–100 slider, the daily counterpart of the 0.3-point SWEMWBS difference behind the preregistered SESOI) would require `r txt_d_hours_to_mid` additional hours of same-day play, and under the hierarchical prior the daily within-person genre spread implies an expected `r txt_d_tau_w_n_genres` of the 14 genres more than one slider point per hour from the common genre effect. Therefore, moving the measurement closer in time, on its own, does not conjure a meaningful effect.

## Are all games the same?

The question this study set out to answer rests on an undisputed fact, that games differ psychologically, and although current genre labels are not an effective way to operationalise those differences when it comes to wellbeing outcomes, the general intuition persists. Game scholars have argued for decades that genre labels are conventions of marketing and library organisation rather than coherent descriptions of play: they conflate gameplay style, purpose, and mood in a single word [@leeFacetAnalysisVideo2014], fail elementary classificatory tests [@clarkeWhyVideoGame2017], and drift as the medium evolves [@cohenHistoryGenre1986; @vargas-iglesiasMakingSenseGenre2020]. Even the literature most committed to genre-specific effects has reached the same conclusion: the researchers who documented attentional benefits of action games now argue that industry genre labels have become poor proxies for the mechanics that produce those benefits, and call for a taxonomy of the processes engaged during play instead [@bavelierEnhancingAttentionalControl2019; @nguyenPlayVideoGames2023]. Games within one genre can differ sharply in structure, as Call of Duty and Halo do within the shooter genre [@sainiInvestigatingGamingStructural2023]. The pathways plausibly connecting play to wellbeing seem to operate at levels that genre labels cannot index [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. For example, need satisfaction depends on autonomy-supportive design features [@ballouBasicNeedsGames2023; @pengNeedSatisfactionSupportive2012], social capital depends on co-play relationships [@depping2018friendship; @vellaPlayingAlonePlaying2015a], and affect regulation depends on the match between gameplay and current emotional state [@kosa2020escapism].

The broader point is that, as many have argued theoretically but have lacked empirical data to show conclusively, other aspects of game play besides genre are likely more meaningful for wellbeing. Structural characteristics (e.g., avatar customisability) are one such aspect, and dedicated taxonomies now exist for characterising these [e.g., @sainiInvestigatingGamingStructural2023]. In-game behaviour is another: within a single game, behavioural variation in how people play is linked to meaningful wellbeing differences even when genre is held constant [e.g., @hakman2026notallplay]. How players fit gaming into their lives is a third: among casual Nintendo players, self-rated gaming life fit predicted wellbeing an order of magnitude more strongly than any playtime measure [@ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. Community-assigned tags that describe mechanics, themes, and social structure may offer a practical middle ground between genre labels and title-level coding [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @liFactororientedUnderstandingVideo2020].

Our data leave two parts of this picture untested. Mobile games were recorded only as daily minutes without titles; they enter only the first positive control and the preregistered all-platform H1 test in Appendix D, which likewise finds no practically significant association, and none of the genre analyses (see Limitations). Monetisation is the other: free-to-play models, loot boxes, and the related design features that have been argued to harm players [@rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021; @sainiInvestigatingGamingStructural2023] need not be spread evenly across genres, so a genre contrast may partly carry a monetisation contrast; in one clinical sample the two were entangled closely enough that the authors proposed monetisation model as the more tractable partition [@andreRelationshipGameGenre2024].

## Methodological Contribution: A Model for Overlapping Categories

Methodologically, the multi-membership model transfers beyond games. To our knowledge this is the first application in media psychology of the model class, developed originally for educational data where students attend multiple schools [@fielding2006cross; @cafri2015introduction]. Any media effects question with overlapping content labels has the same structure (e.g., streaming titles with multiple genre tags, news diets spanning outlets with overlapping orientations, social media feeds spanning topic categories) and can be answered with the same model. Our code is freely available to support future applications of this method.

## Limitations

Several limitations constrain these conclusions and point at the work that should come next. First, the design is observational. The within-person decomposition removes stable confounds but not time-varying ones, and players themselves name illness, grief, work pressure, and caretaking as events that move both play and wellbeing, sometimes in opposite directions [@ballouIllHealthGrief2025]; our causal statements are correspondingly guarded [@rohrer2023within]. Second, the SWEMWBS is a global instrument assessed over a two-week recall window. Gaming sits alongside factors like sleep, work, and social life for wellbeing variance, and domain-specific outcomes (affect, sleep, connectedness) could show associations a global measure averages away. The exploratory daily analysis takes one step down this temporal hierarchy, but future work should consider pairing session-level telemetry with momentary assessments and using time-use data to partial gaming from competing activities. Third, coverage is imperfect: some participants used additional platforms whose telemetry we could not capture, Nintendo telemetry covers first-party titles only [@ballou2025openplay], the main and genre analyses excluded mobile play, which was recorded only as daily minutes without titles or metadata and enters only the first positive control and the preregistered all-platform H1 test in Appendix D, and in-study minutes are dominated by Steam (`r txt_share_get_Steam`%, versus `r txt_share_get_Xbox`% Xbox and `r txt_share_get_Nintendo`% Nintendo), so the genre findings are predominantly findings about PC play by UK and US adults. Fourth, participants were adults aged 18 to 40 at screening, so our conclusions say nothing about children or adolescents, for whom both play patterns and susceptibility may differ. Nor do they extend to disordered play in clinical or at-risk populations, where genre-linked structural characteristics remain plausibly relevant [@rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021; @andreRelationshipGameGenre2024]. Stated as constraints on generality [@simonsConstraintsGeneralityCOG2017], our conclusions apply to adults aged 18 to 40 in the UK and US, to console and PC play recorded during the Open Play study period, and to the IGDB genre taxonomy; we have no reason to believe they depend on other characteristics of the sample, but they have not been tested beyond it.

# Appendix A: Deviations from Preregistration {.appendix}

This appendix lists all deviations from the Stage 1 preregistration [@ballou2024psychological] in the structured disclosure format of Willroth and Atherton [-@willroth2024reporting]: the original wording, what was done instead, the reason, the timing relative to data access and results, and the impact on interpretation. Analyses that were not preregistered (M3, M4, and the daily-timescale analysis) are not deviations and are labelled exploratory where they appear. Changes made upstream during data collection, outside the authors' control, are consolidated as D6. D7 records a restriction of the analytic sample that followed a correction in a later upstream data release.

| \# | Topic | Type | Timing |
|:-----------------|:-------------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| D1 | Genre assignment by full attribution | Data preparation | After data access, before results known |
| D2 | Genre taxonomy | Data preparation | After data access, before results known |
| D3 | Bayesian estimation and priors | Inferential criteria | After data access, before results known |
| D4 | H1 platform scope without mobile | Variables | After data access, before results known |
| D5 | Missing-data protocol | Analytic approach | After complete-case results known |
| D6 | Upstream data-collection changes | Data collection procedures | During data collection, before data access |
| D7 | Analytic sample restricted to qualified participants | Data exclusions | After data access and after results known |

## Structured disclosures

### D1: Genre assignment by full attribution

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data preparation |
| **Original wording** | Games are classified by their primary (first) IGDB genre. |
| **Deviation description** | A game's full playtime counts towards every one of its IGDB genre labels (up to `r max_raw_labels` per game). Genre hours are therefore exposures to games carrying each label and are not mutually exclusive; total playtime for H1 is computed separately from raw sessions. |
| **Reason** | Most games carry several labels; using only the first discards classification information and depends on IGDB's label order. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results known |
| **Reader impact** | Each genre coefficient estimates the association with exposure to games carrying that label, not the effect of a genre in isolation. Under the preregistered primary-genre attribution, the within-person joint Wald test does not reject the equality of the genre coefficients (*p* = `r txt_reg_p_primary_a`), whereas it does under full attribution (*p* = `r txt_reg_p_main_a`), so the support for H2a depends on this choice (Appendix D, @tbl-frequentist-registered, primary-attribution rows). |

### D2: Genre taxonomy

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data preparation |
| **Original wording** | IGDB sub-genres are collapsed as follows: Hack and slash/Beat 'em up → Action; Point-and-click and Visual Novel → Adventure; Turn-based strategy, Real-time strategy, and Tactical → Strategy; Quiz/Trivia → Puzzle. |
| **Deviation description** | Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up, Point-and-click, and Visual Novel are kept as separate categories; MOBA joins Strategy, Card & Board Game joins Puzzle, Pinball and Music join Arcade, and Indie is dropped as a non-substantive label, giving 14 categories (Appendix B). |
| **Reason** | The preregistered collapsing merged genres that prior literature treats as psychologically distinct. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results known |
| **Reader impact** | Per-genre estimates refer to different category boundaries than the preregistration implies. The retained sub-genres are rarely played and have wide credible intervals. |

### D3: Bayesian estimation and priors

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Inferential criteria |
| **Original wording** | H1: equivalence test (TOST) with SESOI = ±0.06 SWEMWBS points per hour/day, using 90% CIs. H2: joint Wald test via `car::linearHypothesis()`. No priors are specified (all models frequentist). |
| **Deviation description** | M1 and M2 are estimated as Bayesian multilevel models with `brms` [@burkner2017brms] rather than with `lmer`. H1 is evaluated against the preregistered ROPE \[−0.06, +0.06\], with a 95% credible interval entirely inside the ROPE establishing practical equivalence [@kruschke2018rejecting], in place of the preregistered decision grid for the 90% confidence interval (Methods; Appendix D). The preregistered joint Wald test for H2 is retained on the frequentist counterpart of M2 and answers H2; the size of any departure is described, without a verdict, by the posterior SD of M2's genre coefficients and the shares of genres and genre pairs it implies beyond the SESOI (Methods). All priors are the `brms` defaults: improper flat priors on the coefficients, a Student-*t*(3, `r txt_wemwbs_median`, 2.5) prior on the intercept, centred at the sample median of SWEMWBS, and half-Student-*t*(3, 0, 2.5) priors on the standard deviations (Appendix F). An earlier version used weakly informative priors; the switch to the defaults was made after those results were known. |
| **Reason** | Alongside the decision, the ROPE gives a continuous measure of practical equivalence (the posterior share inside it). With flat priors on the slopes, the data alone determine their estimates, so the Bayesian estimates are directly comparable with the preregistered maximum-likelihood analysis. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results known (Bayesian estimation); the switch to the `brms` default priors was made after the results of the earlier priors were known |
| **Reader impact** | The SESOI and the equivalence region are unchanged, so the risk of bias is low. All priors are the `brms` defaults (Appendix F), so no analyst-chosen prior scale enters the models. The preregistered frequentist analyses, with the equivalence tests on 90% confidence intervals and the joint Wald tests, are reported in full in Appendix D (Preregistered Frequentist Analysis, @tbl-frequentist-registered). |

### D4: H1 platform scope without mobile

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Variables |
| **Original wording** | H1 uses total playtime across all five platforms (Nintendo, Xbox, Steam, iOS, Android). |
| **Deviation description** | H1 total playtime uses Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam only. Mobile platforms provide daily minutes without game titles (D6), so including them for H1 but not for H2 would give "total playtime" two different meanings. |
| **Reason** | Consistency between H1 and H2. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results known |
| **Reader impact** | Mobile play is omitted from the H1 exposure; it made up `r txt_reg_pct_mobile_time`% of all-platform playtime in the analysed person-waves, and the preregistered all-platform H1 model likewise finds no practically significant association in either dimension (Appendix D, @tbl-frequentist-registered, all-platform rows). The findings do not speak to mobile play. |

### D5: Missing-data protocol

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Analytic approach |
| **Original wording** | Multiple imputation via `mice` (predictive mean matching, wide format); report both complete-case and imputed results. |
| **Deviation description** | Wave nonresponse rather than item missingness dominates: `r txt_n_md_wave_miss` of `r txt_n_md_grid` person-waves (`r pct_md_wave_miss`%) have no SWEMWBS. We therefore imputed on the full participant × wave grid with two-level MICE (`2l.pmm`, participants as clusters; m = 100 by von Hippel's rule) and report pooled frequentist results alongside the complete-case Bayesian models (Appendix D). |
| **Reason** | Single-level wide-format PMM ignores the hierarchical structure and cannot address wave nonresponse. |
| **Timing** | Adopted after the complete-case results were known; the protocol was taken over unchanged from the sibling Stage 2 studies of the same programmatic report rather than tailored to these results |
| **Reader impact** | The H1 conclusions are unchanged under imputation, whereas the pooled within-person joint test for H2 does not reject the equality of the genre coefficients, unlike the complete-case test; the pooled between-person H1 interval widens because person means are uncertain for participants with few observed waves. Agreement between complete-case and imputed H1 results does not rule out bias from nonresponse that depends on unobserved wellbeing. |

### D6: Upstream data-collection changes

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data collection procedures |
| **Original wording** | Age range 18–75 (UK) and 18–30 (US); at least 75% of gaming time on included platforms; Android telemetry as session-level ActivityWatch exports. |
| **Deviation description** | Made by the Open Play team before this study's data access: screening admitted ages 18–40 in both regions, the coverage threshold was lowered to 50%, and Android data were collected as daily minutes from Digital Wellbeing screenshots. Reported in full by @ballou2025openplay. |
| **Reason** | Recruitment and data-collection constraints upstream; outside the authors' control. |
| **Timing** | During data collection, before data access |
| **Reader impact** | Findings generalise to adults aged 18–40; the lower coverage threshold adds measurement error to total playtime; Android contributes daily totals only (see D4). |

### D7: Analytic sample restricted to qualified participants

| Field | Content |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data exclusions |
| **Original wording** | Those who "(1) self-report playing video games, (2) self-report that at least 75% of their total video game play takes place on the platforms included in the study, and (3) are willing to link all relevant gaming accounts will be invited to complete an intake survey"; participants without playtime logged on any self-reported platform during a 7-day baseline are excluded before the panel surveys. "We do not preregister any further exclusion criteria." |
| **Deviation description** | The analytic sample is restricted to participants whose intake record is flagged as qualified in Open Play v1.2.6. Release v1.2.4 revoked this flag for `r n_revoked_intakes` intakes of participants who had entered the surveys without passing the account-linking and telemetry validation; `r txt_n_revoked_in_sample` of them had been in our earlier analytic sample and are now excluded. The same rule excludes `r txt_n_no_intake_v121` participants of the earlier sample whose biweekly responses carry a participant identifier that matches no intake record in any release. We traced this to the data provider's survey export, which takes the identifier from each survey response without checking it against the intake table, so that responses whose identifier differs from the one on the exported intake record, or whose intake was never completed, appear as participants without a screening record; we reported it to the Open Play team. Their qualification cannot be established from the release, and the cleaned release files hold no console or PC telemetry for them. The analytic sample is `r txt_n_model` participants. |
| **Reason** | An upstream correction of the eligibility flag, described in the release notes as false positives. Most participants whose flag was revoked had not met the preregistered linking and telemetry criteria: of the `r txt_n_revoked_in_sample` in the earlier sample, `r txt_n_revoked_never_linked` had never linked an account and `r txt_n_revoked_no_telemetry` have no console or PC telemetry at all, so their zero playtime was unobserved rather than recorded. The participants without an intake record have no screening record under that identifier and no console or PC telemetry in the cleaned release files, so their exposure is unknown. Retaining either group would have entered missing exposure as zero play. |
| **Timing** | After data access and after the results were known; triggered by the August 2026 data release, not by the results |
| **Reader impact** | The sample is smaller, and estimates refer to participants whose playtime was validly observed. In frequentist refits of the preregistered models on the earlier sample (`r txt_reg_n_v121_pid` participants) and on the corrected sample, the within-person slope is practically unchanged (`r txt_reg_w_v121` and `r txt_reg_w_main`), the between-person slope moves slightly towards zero (from `r txt_reg_b_v121` `r txt_reg_b_v121_ci` to `r txt_reg_b_main` `r txt_reg_b_main_ci`, 90% CIs), the preregistered decision grid gives the same H1 verdicts on both samples (no practically significant association within persons; a negative association that is not practically significant between persons), and both joint Wald tests reach the same decisions (within: *p* = `r txt_reg_p_v121_a` and `r txt_reg_p_main_a`; between: *p* = `r txt_reg_p_v121_b` and `r txt_reg_p_main_b`; Appendix D, @tbl-frequentist-registered). |

# Appendix B: Genre Mapping {.appendix}

Genre labels from all three platforms resolve to the study taxonomy in two steps: Xbox store labels are first mapped onto IGDB genres (per the preregistration's Appendix B), and raw IGDB labels (`r n_raw_genre_labels` distinct labels observed in the study metadata) are then collapsed into 14 analysis-level categories. @tbl-genre-mapping presents both steps in one place: each row is an implemented study genre, with the raw IGDB labels it subsumes, the Xbox store labels routed to it, and, where the preregistered mapping (which would yield `r n_prereg_genres` distinct genres on the observed labels) treated a label differently, the preregistered assignment. The implemented mapping diverges from the preregistered one in both directions: it preserves granularity for sub-genres that prior literature treats as distinct (Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up, Point-and-click, Visual Novel), collapses more aggressively elsewhere (MOBA into Strategy, Card & Board Game into Puzzle, Pinball and Music into Arcade), and excludes Indie as a non-substantive label (see Appendix A, Deviation D2). Two details sit outside the table: the Xbox label Family + Kids has no IGDB equivalent and is resolved by the title's secondary genre, and IGDB includes no top-level "Action" category, so what is colloquially called "action" is distributed across Shooter, Hack-and-slash, Fighting, and Platform.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-genre-mapping
#| tbl-cap: "Mapping from platform genre labels to the 14 study genres. Xbox store labels map onto IGDB genres, which are then collapsed into the study taxonomy. The final column gives the preregistered assignment where it differs; blank cells indicate identical treatment."
#| echo: false

genre_map <- tribble(
  ~`Study genre`, ~`IGDB label(s) subsumed`, ~`Xbox store label(s)`, ~`Preregistered assignment (where different)`,
  "Adventure", "Adventure", "Action + Adventure", "Also subsumes Point-and-click and Visual Novel",
  "Arcade", "Arcade, Pinball, Music", "Classics, Music", "Pinball and Music retained as separate genres",
  "Fighting", "Fighting", "Fighting", "",
  "Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up", "Hack and slash/Beat 'em up", "", "Collapsed into Action",
  "Platform", "Platform", "Platformer", "",
  "Point-and-click", "Point-and-click", "", "Collapsed into Adventure",
  "Puzzle", "Puzzle, Quiz/Trivia, Card & Board Game", "Puzzle + Trivia, Card + Board, Casino", "Card & Board Game retained as a separate genre",
  "Racing", "Racing", "Racing + Flying", "",
  "Role-playing", "Role-playing (RPG)", "Role Playing", "",
  "Shooter", "Shooter", "Shooter", "",
  "Simulator", "Simulator", "Simulation", "",
  "Sport", "Sport", "Sports", "",
  "Strategy", "Strategy, Turn-based strategy (TBS), Real time strategy (RTS), Tactical, MOBA", "Strategy, Multi-Player Online Battle Arena", "MOBA retained as a separate genre",
  "Visual Novel", "Visual Novel", "", "Collapsed into Adventure",
  "(excluded)", "Indie", "", "Retained as Indie"
)

genre_map |>
  tt(width = 1) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(j = 1, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(i = nrow(genre_map), j = 1, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.75)
```

# Appendix D: Sensitivity and Supplementary Analyses {.appendix}

This appendix first reports the preregistered frequentist analyses, on the analytic sample, under two preregistered specifications, and on the earlier sample that Deviation D7 corrects. It then reports the two sensitivity analyses summarised under Robustness in the main text: demographic covariate adjustment and multiple imputation of wave nonresponse (with distributional diagnostics). The predictive model comparison (whether genre terms improve out-of-sample prediction) follows, and finally the design details and sensitivity refits of the daily-timescale analysis.

## Preregistered Frequentist Analysis

The preregistered analyses were frequentist: H1 was to be tested by an equivalence test on the 90% confidence intervals of the within-between model of total playtime, and H2 by joint Wald tests of the equality of the genre coefficients, both on multilevel models fitted with `lme4`. The Bayesian models in the main text are the models we interpret (Deviation D3), and the Results report the preregistered H2 tests on the analytic sample. This subsection reports all preregistered tests in one place (@tbl-frequentist-registered): on the analytic sample, under the two preregistered specifications from which the main analysis departs, total playtime across all five platforms for H1 (Deviation D4) and primary-genre attribution for H2 (Deviation D1), and on the earlier analytic sample that Deviation D7 corrects. The all-platform total adds each wave's iOS and Android gaming minutes to its Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam playtime; `r txt_reg_n_mobile_pids` participants had mobile minutes in at least one analysed person-wave, and `r txt_reg_pct_mobile_pw`% of the analysed person-waves had any. Under primary attribution, each game's full playtime counts towards its first IGDB genre label that remains in the 14-genre taxonomy (Appendix B), so genre exposures are mutually exclusive. The earlier sample comprises the `r txt_reg_n_v121_pid` participants with at least one valid SWEMWBS in Open Play v1.2.1, without the qualification condition, and its analysis frame was built from the v1.2.1 files with the same code as the main frame. Each H1 model has a random intercept and a correlated random slope for within-person playtime, as preregistered, and was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood; each H2 model was fitted by maximum likelihood with a random intercept, because the preregistered uncorrelated random slopes gave a singular fit in all three H2 analyses (table note). H1 verdicts follow the preregistered decision grid of the Stage 1 Design Table, applied to the lower (LB) and upper (UB) bounds of the 90% confidence interval: LB \> 0.06 or UB \< −0.06 indicates a practically significant positive or negative association; LB \> 0 and UB \> 0.06, or UB \< 0 and LB \< −0.06, a positive or negative association that may be practically significant; LB \> 0 and UB \< 0.06, or UB \< 0 and LB \> −0.06, a positive or negative association that is not practically significant; LB \> −0.06 and UB \< 0.06 with an interval that covers zero, no practically significant association; and an interval that covers zero and one or both bounds, an inconclusive result. The Design Table lists the absence of a practically significant association for every interval inside ±0.06, including those that exclude zero, and we applied the more specific classes to the latter; it also gives the first bound as LB \> −0.06, which we read as LB \> 0.06, the counterpart of UB \< −0.06. H2 is supported if the joint test rejects equality at α = .05.

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-frequentist-registered
#| tbl-cap: "Preregistered frequentist analyses on the analytic sample, under the preregistered specifications, and on the earlier sample (D7). H1 rows: within-person (H1a) and between-person (H1b) total-playtime coefficients in SWEMWBS points per hour/day with Wald 90% confidence intervals, classified by the preregistered decision grid (SESOI ±0.06; text above the table). H2 rows: joint Wald tests of the equality of the 14 within-person (H2a) and the 14 between-person (H2b) genre coefficients, with the SD of the 14 coefficient estimates as a descriptive summary."
#| echo: false

reg_spec_h1 <- c("Analytic sample, console/PC", "All five platforms (D4)",
                 "Earlier sample (D7)")
reg_spec_h2 <- c("Analytic sample, full attribution", "Primary attribution (D1)",
                 "Earlier sample (D7)")
reg_h1_rows <- bind_rows(reg_h1_main, reg_h1_allplat, reg_h1_v121) |>
  mutate(Specification = rep(reg_spec_h1, each = 2),
         Test = ifelse(term == "within", "H1a", "H1b"),
         Result = sprintf("%.4f [%.4f, %.4f]", estimate, lo, hi),
         p = "", `Genre SD` = "")
reg_h2_rows <- bind_rows(reg_h2_main, reg_h2_primary, reg_h2_v121) |>
  mutate(Specification = rep(reg_spec_h2, each = 2),
         Test = ifelse(term == "within", "H2a", "H2b"),
         Result = sprintf("χ²(%d) = %.1f", df, chisq),
         p = sprintf("%.3f", p), `Genre SD` = sprintf("%.3f", sd_coef))
bind_rows(reg_h1_rows, reg_h2_rows) |>
  transmute(
    Test, Specification,
    Participants = formatC(n_pid, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `Person-waves` = formatC(n_obs, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `Estimate [90% confidence interval] or χ²` = Result, p, `Genre SD`,
    `Preregistered verdict` = verdict
  ) |>
  tt(notes = sprintf(
    "Analytic sample: qualified participants with at least one valid SWEMWBS (Open Play v1.2.6). Earlier sample: participants with at least one valid SWEMWBS in Open Play v1.2.1, before the correction of Deviation D7. H1 models: random intercept and correlated random slope for within-person playtime, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. H2 models: random intercept, fitted by maximum likelihood; the preregistered structure with uncorrelated random slopes for the 14 within-person genre exposures is singular in all three H2 analyses, with %d (analytic sample, full attribution), %d (primary attribution) and %d (earlier sample) of the 14 slope SDs estimated at zero. Genre SD: SD of the 14 genre coefficient estimates, which includes their estimation error.",
    reg_slopes_n_zero, reg_slopes_primary$n_zero, reg_slopes_v121$n_zero)) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```
:::

Under the preregistered grid, the within-person coefficient on the analytic sample, `r txt_reg_w_main` `r txt_reg_w_main_ci`, showed no practically significant association, and the between-person coefficient, `r txt_reg_b_main` `r txt_reg_b_main_ci`, a negative association that is not practically significant: its interval excluded zero but lay inside ±0.06. The earlier sample gave the same two verdicts. Mobile play made up `r txt_reg_pct_mobile_time`% of all-platform playtime in the analysed person-waves. With it included, the within-person verdict was unchanged, and the between-person interval, `r txt_reg_b_allplat` `r txt_reg_b_allplat_ci`, included zero, so this coefficient showed no practically significant association. None of the `r nrow(reg_h1_all)` H1 rows showed an association that is, or may be, practically significant. On the analytic sample under full attribution, the within-person joint test rejected the equality of the genre coefficients (*p* = `r txt_reg_p_main_a`) and the between-person test did not (*p* = `r txt_reg_p_main_b`), so H2a was supported and H2b was not; the earlier sample gave the same decisions (*p* = `r txt_reg_p_v121_a` and *p* = `r txt_reg_p_v121_b`). Under the preregistered primary-genre attribution, neither test rejected equality (within: χ²(`r txt_reg_df_primary`) = `r txt_reg_chisq_primary_a`, *p* = `r txt_reg_p_primary_a`; between: χ²(`r txt_reg_df_primary`) = `r txt_reg_chisq_primary_b`, *p* = `r txt_reg_p_primary_b`), so the support for H2a depended on the attribution rule. Primary attribution assigns each multi-genre game to a single genre, which leaves genres that are seldom listed first with few players: `r txt_reg_rare_label` was the primary genre of games played by `r txt_reg_rare_n_primary` participants, whereas `r txt_reg_rare_n_full` participants played games carrying the label. Its between-person coefficient had a standard error of `r txt_reg_rare_se`, and the SD of the other 13 between-person coefficients was `r txt_reg_sd_primary_b_wo`, so the between-person SD of `r txt_reg_sd_primary_b` under primary attribution reflected the estimation error of this genre rather than a spread across genres.

## Demographic Covariates

The preregistration specified a sensitivity analysis adjusting the primary models for demographic covariates. We refit M1 (total playtime) and M2 (independent genre coefficients) with age, gender, and ethnicity added as population-level predictors, using the subset of participants with complete demographic data.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-demographics-bayes
#| cache: false   # loads brms fits from models/*.rds; caching would serialise GBs
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| include: false

demo_data <- analysis_data |>
  left_join(analytic_sample |> select(pid, age, gender, ethnicity), by = "pid") |>
  filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(gender), !is.na(ethnicity), !is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  mutate(
    gender    = factor(gender, levels = c("Man", "Woman", "Non-binary/Other")),
    ethnicity = factor(ethnicity, levels = c("White", "Asian", "Black",
                                              "Mixed/Multiple", "Other"))
  )

n_sens_pids <- n_distinct(demo_data$pid)
n_sens_obs  <- nrow(demo_data)

# H1 with demographics (fit cached; see R/fit_sensitivity_models.R)
h1_demo <- brm(
  bf(wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + age + gender + ethnicity +
       (1 + total_within | pid)),
  data    = demo_data,
  # brms default priors, as in M1 and M2 (since 2026-10-13).
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h1_demographics")
)

# H2 with demographics
h2_demo_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~ age + gender + ethnicity +",
  paste(c(gh_within, gh_between), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | pid)"
))

h2_demo <- brm(
  formula = h2_demo_formula,
  data    = demo_data,
  # brms default priors, as in M1 and M2 (since 2026-10-13).
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h2_demographics")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-extract
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# H1 coefficients from the adjusted model
h1_demo_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h1_demo)
sens_b1_draws   <- h1_demo_draws$b_total_within
sens_b1_mean    <- mean(sens_b1_draws)
sens_b1_ci      <- quantile(sens_b1_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sens_b1_in_rope <- mean(sens_b1_draws > -0.06 & sens_b1_draws < 0.06)

sens_b2_draws   <- h1_demo_draws$b_total_between
sens_b2_mean    <- mean(sens_b2_draws)
sens_b2_ci      <- quantile(sens_b2_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sens_b2_in_rope <- mean(sens_b2_draws > -0.06 & sens_b2_draws < 0.06)

# Genre heterogeneity (SD of coefficients per draw) from the adjusted model
h2_demo_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h2_demo)
sens_within_cols  <- grep("^b_gh_.*_within$",  names(h2_demo_draws), value = TRUE)
sens_between_cols <- grep("^b_gh_.*_between$", names(h2_demo_draws), value = TRUE)
sens_sd_within  <- apply(as.matrix(h2_demo_draws[, sens_within_cols]),  1, sd)
sens_sd_between <- apply(as.matrix(h2_demo_draws[, sens_between_cols]), 1, sd)

sens_diag_rhat <- max(
  max(brms::rhat(h1_demo), na.rm = TRUE),
  max(brms::rhat(h2_demo), na.rm = TRUE)
)
sens_diag_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h1_demo), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value) +
  sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_demo), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

sens_h1_max_diff <- max(abs(c(sens_b1_mean - beta1_mean, sens_b2_mean - beta2_mean)))
# Guard for the main-text Robustness claim ("less than 0.01 points").
stopifnot(sens_h1_max_diff < 0.01)
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity-demo
#| tbl-cap: "Primary versus demographic-adjusted estimates. H1 rows compare M1's total-playtime coefficients with the same coefficients after adding age, gender, and ethnicity. H2 rows compare M2's genre heterogeneity statistic (SD of the 14 genre coefficients, computed at each posterior draw) with its adjusted counterpart. Estimates in SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "H1a: Within-person total playtime",
    "H1b: Between-person total playtime",
    "H2a: Genre SD (within)",
    "H2b: Genre SD (between)"
  ),
  `Primary` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", beta1_mean, beta1_ci[1], beta1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", beta2_mean, beta2_ci[1], beta2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", genre_sd_mean, genre_sd_ci[1], genre_sd_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", genre_bsd_mean, genre_bsd_ci[1], genre_bsd_ci[2])
  ),
  `Adjusted` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", sens_b1_mean, sens_b1_ci[1], sens_b1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", sens_b2_mean, sens_b2_ci[1], sens_b2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", mean(sens_sd_within),
            quantile(sens_sd_within, 0.025), quantile(sens_sd_within, 0.975)),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", mean(sens_sd_between),
            quantile(sens_sd_between, 0.025), quantile(sens_sd_between, 0.975))
  )
) |> tt()
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: txt-demographic-covariates-1
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_n_sens_obs <- formatC(n_sens_obs, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
txt_n_sens_pids <- formatC(n_sens_pids, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
txt_sens_h1_max_diff <- round(sens_h1_max_diff, 3)
txt_sens_b1_in_rope_pct <- fmt_rope_pct(sens_b1_in_rope)
txt_sens_b2_in_rope_pct <- fmt_rope_pct(sens_b2_in_rope)
txt_sens_b2_ci_lo <- round(sens_b2_ci[1], 3)
txt_sens_b2_ci_hi <- round(sens_b2_ci[2], 3)
txt_sens_diag_rhat <- round(sens_diag_rhat, 3)
```

The adjusted models used `r txt_n_sens_obs` observations from `r txt_n_sens_pids` participants with complete demographic data. @tbl-sensitivity-demo compares the primary and covariate-adjusted estimates. The H1 coefficients shifted by at most `r txt_sens_h1_max_diff` points after adjustment, and the ROPE conclusions were unchanged: `r txt_sens_b1_in_rope_pct`% of the adjusted within-person posterior draws fell inside the ROPE (primary: `r txt_beta1_in_rope_pct`%), and `r txt_sens_b2_in_rope_pct`% of the adjusted between-person posterior draws (primary: `r txt_beta2_in_rope_pct`%). One qualification: the adjusted between-person credible interval (\[`r txt_sens_b2_ci_lo`, `r txt_sens_b2_ci_hi`\]) excluded zero, unlike the unadjusted interval; this small negative association remained far inside the ROPE and is consistent with the selection account discussed under H1. The genre heterogeneity estimates were likewise essentially unaffected. Both adjusted models converged cleanly (max R-hat = `r txt_sens_diag_rhat`, `r sens_diag_divs` divergent transitions). Demographic composition therefore did not account for the observed associations.

## Multiple Imputation

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-imputation-load
#| include: false

source(here("R/02_impute_wemwbs.R"))

if (!file.exists(IMP_META_PATH) || !file.exists(IMP_LONG_PATH)) {
  # First render on a fresh clone: produces the cached imputation (~20 min)
  impute_wemwbs()
}

imp_meta     <- readRDS(IMP_META_PATH)
imputed_long <- readRDS(IMP_LONG_PATH)
m_imp        <- length(imputed_long)

miss_wave        <- imp_meta$missingness_by_wave
n_grid_cells     <- imp_meta$n_cells
n_grid_missing   <- imp_meta$n_missing
pct_grid_missing <- round(100 * n_grid_missing / n_grid_cells, 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-imputation-models
#| include: false
#| cache: true
#| dependson: "frequentist-registered"

# --- H1 (console/PC total, same specification as M1) ------------------------
# Complete-case comparator: identical lmer on the observed rows only.
h1_imp_fits <- lapply(imputed_long, function(d) {
  suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    lmer(wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + (1 + total_within | pid),
         data = d,
         control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", calc.derivs = FALSE))
  ))
})

h1_cc_data <- imputed_long[[1]] |>
  semi_join(
    analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |> select(pid, wave),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day) |>
  inner_join(
    analysis_data |> select(pid, wave, wemwbs),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_within  = total_hours_per_day - mean(total_hours_per_day),
    total_between = mean(total_hours_per_day)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

h1_cc_fit <- lmer(
  wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + (1 + total_within | pid),
  data = h1_cc_data, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

h1_imp_pool    <- pool(as.mira(h1_imp_fits))
h1_imp_pool_95 <- summary(h1_imp_pool, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
h1_imp_pool_90 <- summary(h1_imp_pool, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90)

# Verdicts from the preregistered decision grid for 90% CIs (reg_h1_verdict(),
# chunk frequentist-registered), as in @tbl-frequentist-registered.
h1_imp_eq <- h1_imp_pool_90 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(term %in% c("total_within", "total_between")) |>
  mutate(verdict = reg_h1_verdict(`5 %`, `95 %`))

h1_cc_ci90 <- confint(h1_cc_fit, parm = c("total_within", "total_between"),
                      level = 0.90, method = "Wald")

# --- H2 (14 genre exposures, same structure as M2; ML for pooled tests) -----
gh_within_f  <- paste(gh_within,  collapse = " + ")
gh_between_f <- paste(gh_between, collapse = " + ")
h2_full_f    <- paste("wemwbs ~", gh_within_f, "+", gh_between_f, "+ (1 | pid)")

fit_h2 <- function(d, f) {
  suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    lmer(f, data = d, REML = FALSE,
         control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", calc.derivs = FALSE))
  ))
}

h2_imp_fits <- lapply(imputed_long, fit_h2, f = h2_full_f)

# Pooled joint tests of coefficient equality: 13 explicit difference
# constraints per dimension, combined across imputations with the D1
# multivariate Wald statistic (mitml::testConstraints).
d1_h2a <- mitml::testConstraints(
  h2_imp_fits, constraints = paste0(gh_within[-1], " - ", gh_within[1]),
  method = "D1")
d1_h2b <- mitml::testConstraints(
  h2_imp_fits, constraints = paste0(gh_between[-1], " - ", gh_between[1]),
  method = "D1")

d1_row <- function(tm) {
  tt <- as.data.frame(tm$test)
  tibble(F = tt[1, 1], df1 = tt[1, 2], df2 = tt[1, 3], p = tt[1, 4],
         riv = tt[1, 5])
}
d1_h2a_row <- d1_row(d1_h2a)
d1_h2b_row <- d1_row(d1_h2b)

# Complete-case H2 comparator: h2_cc_fit, h2_cc_wald_a/b, sd_within_cc and
# sd_between_cc are computed once in the Results (chunk h2-wald) on the
# observed rows and reused here.

# Genre heterogeneity (SD of the 14 within/between coefficient estimates),
# descriptive analogue of M2's posterior heterogeneity statistic
sd_within_imp <- mean(vapply(h2_imp_fits, function(m)
  sd(lme4::fixef(m)[gh_within]), numeric(1)))
sd_between_imp <- mean(vapply(h2_imp_fits, function(m)
  sd(lme4::fixef(m)[gh_between]), numeric(1)))

# --- Guards for the fixed prose below (fail the render if violated) ---------
# H1 (Robustness, Methods Missing Data, D5, text below the table): neither
# pooled coefficient is practically significant under the preregistered grid,
# i.e. both pooled 90% CIs lie inside +-0.06.
stopifnot(all(h1_imp_eq$verdict %in% reg_h1_nps),
          all(h1_imp_eq$`5 %` > -0.06 & h1_imp_eq$`95 %` < 0.06))
stopifnot(d1_h2a_row$p > 0.05, d1_h2b_row$p > 0.05)
# (The guard sd_within_imp < 0.06 was removed on 2026-10-13 with the post-hoc
# H2 verdict: the genre SD is reported descriptively.)
```

```{r}
#| label: txt-multiple-imputation-1
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_n_grid_cells <- formatC(n_grid_cells, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
txt_n_grid_missing <- formatC(n_grid_missing, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
txt_fmi_within <- round(imp_meta$fmi_pilot$fmi[imp_meta$fmi_pilot$term == "tt_within"], 2)
txt_fmi_between <- round(imp_meta$fmi_pilot$fmi[imp_meta$fmi_pilot$term == "tt_between"], 2)
txt_vonhippel_sentence <- if (imp_meta$m_needed > m_imp) sprintf("Von Hippel's rule would require %d imputations for a %.0f%%-stable standard error; with m = %d the achieved coefficient of variation of the pooled standard errors is approximately %.2f, which widens the pooled intervals slightly but does not affect the H1 verdicts.", imp_meta$m_needed, 100 * 0.05, m_imp, imp_meta$se_cv_achieved) else sprintf("This satisfies von Hippel's requirement of %d imputations.", imp_meta$m_needed)
```

The preregistration specified multiple imputation by chained equations with predictive mean matching. We implemented the two-level grid protocol described in Methods (Missing Data): across the `r txt_n_grid_cells`-cell participant × wave grid, `r txt_n_grid_missing` cells (`r pct_grid_missing`%) had no observed SWEMWBS (@tbl-missingness-wave), and m = `r m_imp` imputed datasets were generated. The pilot fractions of missing information for the H1 coefficients were `r txt_fmi_within` (within-person) and `r txt_fmi_between` (between-person): the between-person coefficient depends on person means that are genuinely uncertain for participants with few observed waves, and Rubin's rules propagate that uncertainty into the pooled intervals. `r txt_vonhippel_sentence`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missingness-wave

#| echo: false

miss_wave |>
  transmute(
    Wave = wave,
    Possible = n_possible,
    Observed = n_observed,
    Missing = n_missing,
    `% missing` = pct_missing
  ) |>
  tt() |>
  format_tt(digits = 1) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.85)
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity-imputation
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'sprintf("Complete-case versus multiply imputed estimates (m = %d; Rubin-pooled with Barnard-Rubin degrees of freedom). H1 rows: total-playtime coefficients from the same within-between model fitted by restricted maximum likelihood, with playtime centred over the observed waves of each participant (hence slightly different from the preregistered rows in @tbl-frequentist-registered, which centre over all survey waves), and verdicts from the preregistered decision grid for 90%% confidence intervals (SESOI 0.06; Appendix D). H2 rows: joint tests of genre-coefficient equality (complete-case Wald chi-square; imputed pooled D1 F-test) and the SD of the 14 genre coefficients. The preregistered complete-case tests, with the preregistered specifications, are reported in @tbl-frequentist-registered.", m_imp)'
#| echo: false

h1_rows <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("H1a: Within-person total playtime", "H1b: Between-person total playtime"),
  `Complete-case` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", fixef(h1_cc_fit)["total_within"],
            h1_cc_ci90["total_within", 1], h1_cc_ci90["total_within", 2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", fixef(h1_cc_fit)["total_between"],
            h1_cc_ci90["total_between", 1], h1_cc_ci90["total_between", 2])
  ),
  `Imputed (pooled)` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
            h1_imp_eq$estimate[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_within"],
            h1_imp_eq$`5 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_within"],
            h1_imp_eq$`95 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_within"]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
            h1_imp_eq$estimate[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_between"],
            h1_imp_eq$`5 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_between"],
            h1_imp_eq$`95 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_between"])
  ),
  Verdict = h1_imp_eq$verdict[match(c("total_within", "total_between"), h1_imp_eq$term)]
)

h2_rows <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("H2a: Joint test, within-person genre coefficients equal",
               "H2b: Joint test, between-person genre coefficients equal",
               "Genre SD (within)", "Genre SD (between)"),
  `Complete-case` = c(
    sprintf("chi2(%d) = %.1f, p = %.3f", h2_cc_wald_a$Df[2],
            h2_cc_wald_a$Chisq[2], h2_cc_wald_a$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]),
    sprintf("chi2(%d) = %.1f, p = %.3f", h2_cc_wald_b$Df[2],
            h2_cc_wald_b$Chisq[2], h2_cc_wald_b$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_within_cc),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_between_cc)
  ),
  `Imputed (pooled)` = c(
    sprintf("F(%d, %.0f) = %.2f, p = %.3f", d1_h2a_row$df1, d1_h2a_row$df2,
            d1_h2a_row$F, d1_h2a_row$p),
    sprintf("F(%d, %.0f) = %.2f, p = %.3f", d1_h2b_row$df1, d1_h2b_row$df2,
            d1_h2b_row$F, d1_h2b_row$p),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_within_imp),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_between_imp)
  ),
  Verdict = c("See text", "Not rejected (either)",
              "Descriptive", "Descriptive")
)

bind_rows(h1_rows, h2_rows) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```
:::

@tbl-sensitivity-imputation compares complete-case and pooled imputed results. The H1 conclusions were unchanged: both pooled 90% confidence intervals fell entirely within ±0.06, so under the preregistered grid neither coefficient showed a practically significant association on the imputed data. The between-person interval widened under imputation, reflecting that person-mean wellbeing is uncertain for participants with few observed waves.

```{r}
#| label: txt-multiple-imputation-2
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_sd_within_cc <- round(sd_within_cc, 3)
txt_sd_within_imp <- round(sd_within_imp, 3)
txt_d1_h2a_row_p <- round(d1_h2a_row$p, 3)
txt_d1_h2b_row_p <- round(d1_h2b_row$p, 3)
txt_d1_h2a_row_riv <- round(d1_h2a_row$riv, 2)
```

For H2, the comparison separates the preregistered test from the size of the genre differences. As reported in the Results, the complete-case joint Wald test rejected *exact* equality of the 14 within-person genre coefficients (χ²(`r h2_cc_wald_a$Df[2]`) = `r txt_wald_a_chisq`, *p* = `r txt_wald_a_p`); under the preregistered decision rule this reading is limited to "at least one pair of genres differs", with no pairwise interpretation absent formal post-hoc tests. The SD of the 14 coefficient estimates, which describes the size of the differences and includes their estimation error, was `r txt_sd_within_cc` (complete-case) and `r txt_sd_within_imp` (imputed). On the imputed data the pooled $D_1$ tests rejected neither dimension (within: *p* = `r txt_d1_h2a_row_p`; between: *p* = `r txt_d1_h2b_row_p`), though these tests carried reduced power at this level of missing information (relative increase in variance `r txt_d1_h2a_row_riv` for the within-person constraints). Distributional diagnostics for the imputation are shown in @fig-imp-density. In sum, accounting for wave nonresponse left the H1 conclusion intact, as neither total-playtime coefficient was practically significant, whereas whether the within-person joint test detected genre differences depended on the frame.

### Distributional Diagnostics

The central plausibility check for the imputation model is distributional: imputed wellbeing values should occupy the same range as the observed data and differ from it only in ways explicable by which participants are missing, not by model artefacts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imp-density
#| fig-cap: "*Multiple-Imputation Distributional Diagnostic.* Observed grand-mean-centred SWEMWBS values (black) against imputed values in 20 of the 100 imputed datasets (thin orange); a subset is shown so the observed curve stays visible, and all 100 behave alike."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false

imp_vals_df <- imp_meta$imp$imp$wemwbs_c
n_imp_show  <- 20
stopifnot(ncol(imp_vals_df) >= n_imp_show, nrow(imp_vals_df) > 0)

obs_dens_df <- tibble(wemwbs_c = na.omit(imp_meta$imp$data$wemwbs_c))
imp_dens_df <- imp_vals_df[, seq_len(n_imp_show)] |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "imputation", values_to = "wemwbs_c")

imp_mean_all <- mean(as.matrix(imp_vals_df))
imp_sd_all   <- sd(as.matrix(imp_vals_df))
obs_sd       <- sd(obs_dens_df$wemwbs_c)

# Guards for the fixed prose: imputed values are distributionally close to
# the observed data (centred scale).
stopifnot(abs(imp_mean_all) < 0.1, abs(imp_sd_all - obs_sd) < 0.1)

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = imp_dens_df,
    aes(x = wemwbs_c, group = imputation, colour = "Imputed"),
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_density(
    data = obs_dens_df,
    aes(x = wemwbs_c, colour = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c(
    Observed = "black",
    Imputed  = scales::alpha("#D55E00", 0.4)
  )) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(x = "Grand-mean-centred SWEMWBS", y = "Density") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
txt_n_imp_shown <- ncol(imp_vals_df)
txt_imp_mean_all <- sprintf("%.3f", imp_mean_all)
```

@fig-imp-density shows the imputed values to be distributionally almost indistinguishable from the observed data: pooled across all `r txt_n_imp_shown` imputations, the imputed values had mean `r txt_imp_mean_all` and SD `r txt_imp_sd_all` on the centred scale, against an observed mean of 0 (by construction) and SD of `r txt_obs_sd`. The imputation model neither compressed the outcome's variance nor shifted nonresponders' imputed wellbeing to implausible regions of the scale. Convergence traces and strip plots are produced alongside the cached imputation (`output/qc_imputation/`).

## Predictive Model Comparison

A complementary way to ask whether genre matters is through predictive performance: does adding genre-specific terms to the total-playtime-only M1 baseline improve out-of-sample prediction? We assessed this using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling [@vehtari2017practical]. A positive difference in expected log predictive density (ELPD) relative to M1 indicates that genre terms help.

```{r}
#| label: loo-comparison
#| cache: true
#| eval: true
#| include: false

# LOO for each model. Computing it here builds draws x observations
# log-likelihood matrices on top of the loaded fits (memory: see CLAUDE.md),
# so the refit script precomputes it to models/loo_*.rds; the render reads
# those files when all four exist and computes LOO itself only otherwise.
# Note: moment_match = TRUE requires a valid compiled Stan object, which
# may not survive caching across sessions. Using standard LOO instead.
# If Pareto-k warnings appear, consider reloo = TRUE as a fallback.
loo_files <- here("models", c("loo_h1.rds", "loo_h2_fe.rds", "loo_h2_mm.rds", "loo_h2_hier.rds"))
if (all(file.exists(loo_files))) {
  loo_h1      <- readRDS(loo_files[1])
  loo_h2_fe   <- readRDS(loo_files[2])
  loo_h2_mm   <- readRDS(loo_files[3])
  loo_h2_hier <- readRDS(loo_files[4])
  # Precomputed objects must belong to the current fits: brms model names
  # (used by loo_compare() and the labels below) and observation counts.
  stopifnot(
    identical(
      vapply(list(loo_h1, loo_h2_fe, loo_h2_mm, loo_h2_hier),
             function(l) as.character(attr(l, "model_name")), character(1)),
      c("h1_model", "h2_model", "h2_mm_model", "h2_hier_model")
    ),
    nrow(loo_h1$pointwise)      == nobs(h1_model),
    nrow(loo_h2_fe$pointwise)   == nobs(h2_model),
    nrow(loo_h2_mm$pointwise)   == nobs(h2_mm_model),
    nrow(loo_h2_hier$pointwise) == nobs(h2_hier_model)
  )
} else {
  loo_h1      <- loo(h1_model)
  loo_h2_fe   <- loo(h2_model)
  loo_h2_mm   <- loo(h2_mm_model)
  loo_h2_hier <- loo(h2_hier_model)
}

loo_comp <- loo_compare(loo_h1, loo_h2_fe, loo_h2_mm, loo_h2_hier)

# Pareto-k diagnostics across the four models (reported in the text)
pareto_k_all <- lapply(list(loo_h1, loo_h2_fe, loo_h2_mm, loo_h2_hier),
                       function(l) l$diagnostics$pareto_k)
pareto_pct_bad <- 100 * vapply(pareto_k_all, function(k) mean(k > 0.7), numeric(1))
pareto_n_bad   <- vapply(pareto_k_all, function(k) sum(k > 0.7), numeric(1))

loo_tbl <- as.data.frame(loo_comp) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("model_label") |>
  mutate(
    model = case_when(
      grepl("h1_model", model_label)      ~ "M1: Total playtime only",
      grepl("h2_model$", model_label)      ~ "M2: Independent coefficients",
      grepl("h2_hier_model", model_label) ~ "M3: Hierarchical prior",
      grepl("h2_mm_model", model_label)   ~ "M4: Multi-membership",
      TRUE ~ model_label
    )
  ) |>
  select(model, elpd_diff, se_diff, elpd_loo, se_elpd_loo, p_loo, looic) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1))) |>
  rename(
    Model = model, `dELPD` = elpd_diff, `SE(d)` = se_diff,
    ELPD = elpd_loo, SE = se_elpd_loo, `p_loo` = p_loo, LOOIC = looic
  )
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-out cross-validation. Models ordered by expected log predictive density (ELPD); negative dELPD indicates worse out-of-sample prediction than the best-fitting model. SE(d) = standard error of the difference."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

loo_tbl |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: txt-predictive-model-comparison-1
#| include: false

# Inline quantities for the paragraph(s) below, defined once here so the
# prose reads `r name` rather than a formatting call.
txt_min_pareto_pct_bad <- round(min(pareto_pct_bad), 1)
txt_max_pareto_pct_bad <- round(max(pareto_pct_bad), 1)
txt_min_pareto_n_bad <- round(min(pareto_n_bad))
txt_max_pareto_n_bad <- round(max(pareto_n_bad))
txt_d_ar1 <- round(d_ar1, 2)
txt_d_r1a_b1 <- round(d_r1a$b1, 2)
txt_d_r1a_b1_ci_lo <- round(d_r1a$b1_ci[1], 2)
txt_d_r1a_b1_ci_hi <- round(d_r1a$b1_ci[2], 2)
txt_d_r1w_b1 <- round(d_r1w$b1, 2)
txt_d_r1w_b1_ci_lo <- round(d_r1w$b1_ci[1], 2)
txt_d_r1w_b1_ci_hi <- round(d_r1w$b1_ci[2], 2)
txt_d_rx_b1 <- round(d_rx_b1, 2)
txt_d_rx_b1_ci_lo <- round(d_rx_b1_ci[1], 2)
txt_d_rx_b1_ci_hi <- round(d_rx_b1_ci[2], 2)
```

M1, the model with total playtime only, showed the highest expected log predictive density, and all three genre specifications predicted slightly worse out-of-sample (@tbl-loo-comparison), with ELPD deficits between one and roughly two standard errors of the difference. Adding genre information, in any of the three specifications, therefore did not improve the prediction of wellbeing over total playtime alone. Pareto-$k$ diagnostics flagged `r txt_min_pareto_pct_bad`–`r txt_max_pareto_pct_bad`% of observations per model ($k$ \> 0.7; `r txt_min_pareto_n_bad`–`r txt_max_pareto_n_bad` observations), so the ELPD values are approximate; this affects the precision of the differences, not the ordering.

## Daily-Timescale Analysis: Design Details and Sensitivity Analyses

Local time was taken from each participant's reported timezone; Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps (8% of sessions) had their minutes spread uniformly over the recorded day. Exclusions from the analysed daily sample were dominated by days without telemetry coverage; excluded responses entered an all-responses sensitivity refit that retains every response and scores unobserved play as zero. Between-person terms are habitual full-day hours, a participant's total telemetry over their observed diary period divided by days. The SESOI for the slider and the choice of its minimally important difference are described in Methods (Daily Timescale).

Four sensitivity refits accompany the exploratory daily analysis. Allowing first-order autocorrelated residuals with a within-person day trend (estimated AR(1) = `r txt_d_ar1`) widened the within-person interval past zero (β = `r txt_d_r1a_b1`, 95% CI \[`r txt_d_r1a_b1_ci_lo`, `r txt_d_r1a_b1_ci_hi`\]), as did adjusting for window length (β = `r txt_d_r1w_b1`, 95% CI \[`r txt_d_r1w_b1_ci_lo`, `r txt_d_r1w_b1_ci_hi`\]). Excluding the 8% of Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps, whose start times were floored to midnight and whose minutes were spread uniformly over the recorded day, left the within-person interval above zero (β = `r txt_d_rx_b1`, 95% CI \[`r txt_d_rx_b1_ci_lo`, `r txt_d_rx_b1_ci_hi`\]). The all-responses refit, which retains every diary response and scores unobserved play as zero, gave the same between-person lean as the analysed sample (β = `r txt_d_r1f_b2`, 95% CI \[`r txt_d_r1f_b2_ci_lo`, `r txt_d_r1f_b2_ci_hi`\]). One qualification applies to the daily genre-level intervals: they inherit the exchangeable-residual assumption that the autocorrelation refit relaxes for the total-playtime model only. Like M3, the daily hierarchical-prior model was estimated in non-centred form; with the same sampler settings as M3 it produced `r txt_d_m3_divs` divergent transition`r if (d_r3$divs == 1) '' else 's'`, against `r d_m3_divs_centred` in the centred form at the stricter adapt_delta of 0.9995.
